#5563. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5562. Homebuilder Stocks Surge as Democratic Sweep Raises Hopes for Affordability Gains

Homebuilders and housing suppliers saw significant jumps in their share prices following the stunning success of Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

At the closing bell on Wednesday, shares of major builders Lennar and PulteGroup were up more than 7% on the day, and D.R. Horton rose more than 8%.

Suppliers showed similar increases. Home Depot finished the day up 6.5%, after spiking as much as 17% during midday trading, according to Yahoo Finance. Lowe’s Companies ended the day up 7.5%, but also had a midday spike to 15% before giving back some gains.

For comparison, the broad S&P 500 index ended the day up 1.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3%, or more than 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since April 2025.

The stock market surge comes in the wake of Tuesday’s midterm election, where Democrats gained control of Congress in a dramatic sweep.

The homebuilding sector has faced massive cost increases in recent years. Several factors have played into the building sector’s hardships, which have led to a shortfall of roughly 4 million homes throughout the U.S., according to a March report from Realtor.com®.

Tariffs, supply chain issues, and inflation have caused substantial increases in material costs, according to Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial Group.

“Labor continues to be a major issue, with a shortage of skilled workers driving wages higher,” Gestiehr tells Realtor.com. “Add in land prices, permitting, insurance, and financing costs, and it becomes increasingly difficult to build homes at prices the average buyer can afford.”

Builders have experienced a squeeze from both sides, Gestiehr explains, because at the same time that the cost to build a home has increased, skyrocketing mortgage rates have put limits on what buyers can afford.

Just days ago, major builders including D.R. Horton and the PulteGroup reported net income declines, with PulteGroup CEO Ryan Marshall stating that the company’s year-over-year net income dropped by 17% in the third quarter.

Suddenly, there’s a renewed sense of optimism surrounding the industry after Tuesday’s election results.

While the underlying challenges remain, Gestiehr says that investors are likely expecting more federal attention to turn to policies surrounding affordability.

“Housing affordability has become a major concern, and investors may be anticipating more attention on policies that encourage new construction and make homeownership more affordable,” says Gestiehr. “Investors may be anticipating additional housing incentives, policies that encourage new construction, and potentially lower mortgage rates.”

Affordability, particularly when it comes to housing, was a key part of many Democratic candidate platforms.

To address affordability overall, there should be focus on building up the supply of homes before offering incentives for buyers and spurring more demand, says Gestiehr.

"If you increase demand without increasing supply, you may end up pushing home prices even higher,” adds Gestiehr. “Reducing regulatory costs, streamlining permitting, encouraging additional development, and potentially lowering tariffs on building materials could all help builders.”

Rolling back tariffs was a major talking point for several incoming Democrat senators, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Texas’ James Talarico, as well as Alaska’s Mary Peltola, whose race results were pending.

Gestiehr maintains that many other factors, including inflation, interest rates, employment, and corporate earnings, as well as actual policy changes, will still have a much greater impact on homebuilder results than the election results alone. It’s not uncommon for markets to perform well following midterm elections, in part because the uncertainty surrounding the election is removed.

“The election may have given homebuilders a reason to be optimistic, but optimism doesn't necessarily translate into stronger earnings,” says Gestiehr. “At some point, these companies need to see improvement in demand, affordability, and profit margins to justify higher stock prices.”

Congress already passed one major bipartisan housing bill this year, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. The bill lays out 45 provisions aimed at cutting red tape and constructing more homes, as well as banning institutional investor homebuyers.

Adding new members to Congress, many of whom have been elected on the promise of ushering in affordability, could mean more meaningful change is on the way.

“With a divided government, I wouldn’t expect major changes overnight, but housing affordability is an area where both parties have an incentive to find common ground,” says Gestiehr.

#5561. October Builder Sentiment: Demand Headwinds Continue

Each month, Zonda surveys builders across the country to gauge sentiment around the housing market. This survey is intended to supplement Zonda’s proprietary database by asking builders more qualitative questions.

The anonymous survey covers everything from consumer sentiment to broader macroeconomic topics like tariffs and immigration. Results are tracked over time and analyzed geographically to capture real-time shifts in builder and consumer confidence.

#5560. Former Landsea Homes President and COO Mike Forsum to Lead New Land Finance Platform

Home building industry veteran Mike Forsum has been tapped to lead a new land finance platform aimed at providing public and private home builders and developers with more flexible capital options.

Wafra, a New York-based global alternative investment manager, and Hunt Cos., a privately held real estate and investment company, have launched Strata Land Partners, with Forsum serving as CEO.

The platform has launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and is designed to serve as a long-term capital partner for builders navigating land investment and development in an uncertain housing market.

Forsum brings more than 40 years of home building industry experience to the venture. Most recently, he served as president and chief operating officer of Landsea Homes. His experience navigating builders’ operational challenges and investment decisions will help shape Strata’s approach.

“Strata was built by builders, for builders,” Forsum said. “Having spent my career in home building, it is apparent that there is significant demand for a strategic capital partner that understands the industry’s operational nuances and thoughtfully supports builders in achieving their goals.”

He added that the platform’s goal is to “bridge that gap and play our part in building the new homes this country needs.”

Strata enters the market as builders look for ways to manage land exposure and capital requirements. According to the announcement, the platform will focus on tailored financing solutions that allow builders and developers to navigate changing market conditions while advancing residential projects.

Ryan Brenner, managing director and head of alternative real estate at Wafra, said Strata is also intended to help address the nation’s structural housing shortage by giving builders another source of capital to support new-home development.

For Hunt Cos., the partnership combines flexible capital with an operating team experienced in residential development.

“Strata brings together an experienced operating team and flexible capital to address a critical need in residential development,” said Chris Hunt, CEO of Hunt Cos. “We look forward to supporting the platform as it builds lasting relationships with home builders and developers nationwide.”

#5559. Inside the $8.9 Million Dallas Treehouse Estate Modeled After a Nautilus Shell, Complete With a Natatorium

A Preston Hollow estate modeled after a nautilus shell is back on the market in Dallas—this time asking $8,875,000.

The property at 5110 Park Lane has been on and off the market since May, when it debuted at $9,999,000.

The residence, a "limestone-and-copper nautilus" by architect Michael Murphy, totals more than 17,000 square feet across the 14,921-square-foot main house and a 2,378-square-foot attached natatorium. The estate is represented by Faisal Halum of Compass RE Texas.

Even in a neighborhood as prestigious as Preston Hollow, where residents have included former President George W. Bush and Mark Cuban, the design of the estate is anything but conventional. Wedge-shaped rooms fan outward from a central elevator, an arrangement meant to give every room a view. With the house set among mature trees, the effect is something like living in a treehouse, suspended in the canopy.

The 1.67-acre lot features rolling terrain, dense foliage, and a creek that winds through the grounds. Warm-toned Lueders limestone, quarried in Texas specifically for the project, carries from the exterior into the interiors, blurring the line between the two.

The primary living quarters occupy the upper level, where buffed concrete floors and Venetian plaster walls are paired with more limestone. Three bedrooms are in the main residence, and a separate guest apartment adds two more. There are five full bathrooms and four half-baths.

The lower level was built for both work and play. It holds office space, media rooms, conference areas, and a workout room, along with the natatorium—where a lap pool features a waterfall lit by fiber optics. The grounds are enclosed by a gated wrought-iron fence, and there is parking for five vehicles.

Dallas Love Field is also nearby, making the home convenient for part-time residents or frequent travelers.

#5558. United Wholesale Mortgage Pushes Through Q3 Amid Headwinds, Predicts Steady Q4

Despite having lower margins for the third quarter, United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) Chairman, President and CEO Mat Ishbia stated that he feels prepared to handle “headwinds in the industry” during the company’s third quarter earnings call.

On the call, Ishbia referenced the challenges the mortgage market has faced within the past five years, saying that the market is “showing a lot of warts on a lot of different companies.”

“Everyone’s got some issue,” he stated. “A lot of other people are operating holes where they don’t have enough business. They don’t have enough opportunity to get loans, they can’t keep up production and they can’t invest in AI.”

Interest rates have weighed on the housing market heavily as of late, leaving mortgage lenders with lower demand. For UWM’s earnings however, Ishbia attributes the company’s success to the recent Oaktree partnership, which came together after an ugly bidding war with CrossCountry Mortgage.

“The best way to hedge is to do a lot more loans when rates drop, as long as you can stomach the Mortgage Servicing Right (MSR) values going down because rates drop,” Ishbia added. “We have a great hedging policy and process. We partnered with Oaktree on that and Vandy Fartaj. We feel really good about the process of how we’re hedging and how much to hedge, versus how much not to hedge.”

The latest Federal Reserve meeting in October concluded with no changes to rates, but mortgage rates have slowly begun to inch downward to the lower 7% range—around 7.24% according to Freddie Mac—after spiking dramatically from the September meeting’s rate hike.

“I think the natural hedge is the best way to do it, and we’re not back to the natural hedge yet,” he said.

Although the quarter’s loan origination volume came in at $33.4 billion—down from Q2 which was $39.7 billion, and the first quarter at $44.9 billion—Ishbia mentioned that expenses were down substantially, specifically tied into investments with AI technology.

“Those (expenses) are really just tied to the investments we’ve made in AI and technology over the last couple years when everyone thought our expenses were higher,” he noted. “And so we’re starting to see the fruits of our labor.”

In total, Q3 revenue clocked in around $811.1 million, which is down from last quarter’s $888 million and slightly down from last year’s revenue of around $843 million.

Adjusted EBITDA came in at $178.3 million, less than last quarter and last year’s estimates ($185.9 million and $211.1 million, respectively).

UWM’s stock grew following the earnings call, as the earnings report beat out expectations. The company’s stock jumped nearly 13%, but is still down about 59% year to date.

Net loss was down quarterly in Q3, to $212.6 million compared to Q2 at $451.9 million. It was significantly higher than last year’s Q3 net loss however ($12.1 million). As an improvement from the previous quarter, Ishbia again credits the lower expenses to the company’s AI investments now panning out.

“AI can definitely help you cut costs and expenses, and you’re seeing some of that benefit, but you have to make a massive investment in it to do that. As you can see, it helps you do more loans, grow your business and drive the top line revenue,” he commented.

As for market share, Ishbia emphasizes the power and role brokers play in UWM’s success. He described brokers as the “growing channel” and states that they are the “winners right now.”

“UWM’s market share is fantastic. We’re strong, we’re dominant, and we’re going to continue to grow. If we lose market share, I hope that happens because that means the broker market has gotten so big and it’s going to keep growing, that’s my focus,” he continued. “My focus is growing the broker channel, helping every loan officer do a little bit more loans, helping every real estate agent that works with brokers do more business, and helping them all win.”

With 2026 winding down, Ishbia sees the upcoming year as a time of “optimization” but said he expected the mortgage market to remain tough for some time. He also notes that UWM focuses primarily on purchase mortgages, and acknowledges the challenges that refinance mortgage loans could face with current rates.

“Since we’re mostly purchase, I’m not as concerned about the volume going down as much as a lot of refinance shops will,” he concluded. “Traditionally, the fourth quarter and first quarter are always the tougher times in the mortgage market. But once again, expenses are down, AI is winning and brokers are growing. We feel like we’re in the best position of anybody to capitalize on opportunity.”

#5557. Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics

Ocient Inc., the maker of a speedy data analytics platform, today said it has raised $100 million in a Series C funding to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business.

That business is fueled by growing demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers seeking to analyze massive datasets without sampling. The new round brings the Chicago-based company’s total funding to $260 million.

Ocient said it expects revenue to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling revenue the previous year. The company said the new financing will accelerate delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions, which enable AI agents and human analysts to query petabyte-scale datasets.

Chief Executive John Morris said much of the growth is coming from new customers in national security and telecommunications, particularly organizations using the platform to consolidate cybersecurity information.

“They’ve been accustomed to having to sample data coming off the network,” Morris said. “They don’t have anything that can handle the ingest rates, nor that can store at an affordable price tens of petabytes of data.”

Ocient’s original business focused on high-performance analytics, but the emergence of AI agents has expanded its potential market. Increasingly, software agents rather than human analysts are querying its systems, driving higher utilization and creating demand for more comprehensive datasets.

The OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration. Its architecture minimizes data movement and uses forward error correction instead of conventional replication to provide data protection with reduced storage overhead.

“The architecture is designed not to move data around constantly as most architectures do, and to have nothing replicated,” Morris said.

The company competes with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and open-source analytics implementations, although its technology frequently complements existing platforms rather than replacing them, the CEO said.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a particularly promising market. Ocient provides the underlying data infrastructure that enables security tools and AI agents to analyze network activity across complete historical datasets, potentially identifying threats that conventional sampling would miss.

However, Morris said the company isn’t positioned as a cybersecurity tool. “We don’t do the detection algorithms and the sort of things that the companies in that space do,” Morris said.

Government and defense customers account for a substantial portion of Ocient’s business. The company recently established a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve those markets.

Morris said the new funding should be sufficient to help Ocient reach breakeven, although he declined to provide a timetable. Ocient plans to direct much of the investment toward hiring sales and customer delivery personnel while continuing engineering development.

The company is also seeing increasing demand for on-premises deployments as customers seek greater control over costs and sensitive information. “Most of our opportunities now are on-prem because they’re either repatriating for cost reasons or for data sovereignty and data protection issues,” Morris said.

The company is also looking to expand geographically, particularly in Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, while pursuing additional cybersecurity customers.

The round was co-led by Boka Capital Ltd. and OCA Ventures LLC, with participation from previous investors Greycroft Partners LLC, In-Q-Tel Inc., Blue Bear Capital LLC, Buoyant Ventures Management LLC, PSP Partners LLC’s PSP Growth fund and Pritzker Group Venture Capital LLC.

#5556. Where Health Care Employment Has the Biggest Footprint

Health care is more than a service for residents. It is also an important piece of the employment landscape. Preliminary August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows significant differences in both the number of health care and social assistance jobs across states and the industry’s share of total employment.

In absolute terms, the country’s largest states naturally account for some of the biggest health care workforces. Unsurprisingly, California leads with over 3.18 million health care and social assistance jobs, followed by New York at 1.91 million and Texas at 1.76 million.

However, the health care industry’s share of a state’s total employment base may tell a different and potentially more useful story.

West Virginia stands at the top of the list, with health care and social assistance representing approximately 19.6% of total employment. New York follows at 19.1%, with Pennsylvania at 18.9%. Connecticut, Minnesota, and Massachusetts are also among the states where the industry accounts for a comparatively large share of employment, at roughly 18.1%, 17.9%, and 17.8%, respectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, health care represents just 8.8% of employment in Wyoming, 10.6% in the District of Columbia and Nevada, 10.8% in Alabama, and 11% in South Carolina.

That variation matters because a sizable health care sector can serve as an important economic anchor, providing a meaningful source of jobs that support the broader housing market.

Access to health care might become an increasingly relevant consideration in retirement location decisions. Affordability matters, but so do physician availability, provider access, and the distance residents need to travel for care.

Demographic trends reinforce that dynamic. Per the U.S. Census Bureau, the old-age dependency ratio, which measures the number of adults age 65+ relative to the working-age population, rose from 20.8 in 2010 to 29.7 in 2024, pointing to future pressure on health care systems, retirement programs, and elder care resources.

As the population ages, health care will matter to housing markets from both an economic and demographic perspective. The sector supports local employment, while access to care can influence where older households choose to live.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5555. Trend of the Month: 6 Ways Floor Plans Are Changing

Current floor plan trends don’t necessarily bring anything brand new to home design, but rather represent subtle shifts to better support how people want to live in their homes today.

Functionality and flow are driving many of the current trends, including these six:

As a result, floor plans are balancing the benefits of open-plan living with spaces that permit partial or total separation from the main living areas. Ideally, a floor plan lets a homeowner choose.

While the kitchen and adjacent living areas remain open, “what is changing is everything around that center. Homeowners still want visual generosity and togetherness, but they also need places for focused work, calls, study, rest, hobbies, or simply a quiet moment,” says Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture.

The key, says Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture, is not to treat open and closed spaces as opposites.

The most desirable plans “create layers between fully shared and fully enclosed space, so homeowners can adjust the degree of connection throughout the day,” says Julian.

Meanwhile, “Smaller cozy corners can remain open to the main space while using placement, furniture, partial screens, or an offset opening to create a sense of retreat,” says Wagner.

Away rooms are trending, which are simply secondary living spaces set off the main living area, with a closing door, and often increased soundproofing, devoted to peace and quiet.

Back kitchens and sculleries physically separate food prep, appliances and cleanup from the main kitchen, where much of daily living and entertaining takes place.

Upstairs retreats, homework rooms, and secondary living spaces create further separation, giving household members somewhere to do their own thing without sacrificing the openness of the kitchen and great room.

Wet rooms are not a new feature but are gaining more attention and are influencing bathroom layouts and design, no longer reserved just for higher-end homes.

“One reason is that you can use every inch of that space, which can mean a larger shower and a more spa-like feel,” says Debra Purvis with Design House.

A wet room typically is an open-concept bathroom, where a bathtub and a shower share an enclosure, sometimes separated by a glass partition from the rest of the bathroom.

Wet rooms offer great decorative potential too, with soaker tubs, steam showers, and statement fixtures. They also lend themselves naturally to other trends like tile drenching, which provides a dramatic, upscale look.

They are family friendly too. “Kids splash water out of the tub; it’s not a problem. Between the tile and floor drains, you are covered,” says Purvis.

Flex rooms offer opportunity in a floor plan without adding square footage, one reason they remain among the most sought-after features in new homes. But today’s buyers are looking for flex rooms with purpose, rather than just a blank-slate bonus room.

Practical considerations, such as outlets, storage, layered lighting, and easy access without crossing through other spaces, offer flexible futureproofing. The flex room needs to be appropriately sized and configured for the potential use too.

Location in the home indicates flex room potential too.

While two-story floor plans remain in-demand, one-story floor plans are showing modest growth.

“A one-story plan is going to be more accessible, generally speaking, which opens it up to buyers in many different life phases,” says Aurora Zeledon, director of digital content and marketing for Zonda House Plans, including Houseplans.com.

While land availability and cost might be driving the uptick in one-story floor plans, the versatility of living on one level has design upside and broad-based appeal, including 55+, multigen households, and younger families who appreciate having everyone on the same level.

One-story plans offer easier circulation, without stairs and landings occupying transitional spaces. Typically, one-story homes benefit from a stronger indoor/outdoor connection, often an anchor of the design, an in-demand feature as well.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), two-story plans still accounted for over half of single-family home starts in 2025 nationwide, although that number had dropped slightly, while the number of single-story homes inched up. Notably, there were significant differences across regions.

Meanwhile, Zeledon reports that the majority of floor plans they have sold, dating back to 2019, are for one-story homes, including their current bestseller. However, she notes that year-to-date there has been a modest increase in one-story house plan sales, compared to last year, pointing out that much of the activity is concentrated in the South and Southeast.

As homes generally scale down in size, storage becomes essential for homeowners to retain the functionality of a larger home in a smaller footprint.

“The overarching idea is to utilize every square foot. When storage is thoughtfully integrated into the architecture, we can maximize the home for multiple purposes—and, importantly, multiple storage solutions—without making the spaces feel overly utilitarian,” says Hannah Sloan, creative marketing specialist with Unscripted Interior Design.

She reports that drop zones are gaining attention, as are Costco closets, laundry/mudroom and owner’s entrances.

Sloan says that some rooms are benefiting from space-specific storage that improves functionality, like in the primary bathroom with more thoughtfully designed vanities and built-ins. Meanwhile, fitness closets are appearing in home gyms to free up floor space for exercise.

“Then there are the found spaces—under-stair book nooks, hidden speakeasy-inspired bars, and other whimsical design opportunities. These spaces can become highly functional while also adding personality and surprise to a home,” says Sloan.

#5554. The Home Depot Foundation Expands Veteran Housing Commitment to $1 Billion

The Home Depot Foundation is increasing its total commitment to veteran causes to $1 billion through 2032, expanding investments in programs designed to address veteran homelessness, housing insecurity, and home accessibility.

Since 2011, the foundation says it has invested more than $650 million in veteran causes and helped improve more than 70,000 veteran homes and facilities. Its latest commitment will combine established housing programs with efforts to test and scale new approaches to veteran housing.

“We believe every veteran deserves a safe place to call home,” said Erin Izen, executive director of The Home Depot Foundation. “Our $1 billion commitment supports the partnerships and solutions needed to help more veterans move from uncertainty to long-term stability.”

Among the initiatives receiving support are programs designed to remove barriers to rental housing. The Landlords, Organizations, and Veterans Engagement (LOVE) Fund, with Open Doors Atlanta, and the U.S. VETS Master Lease Program aim to speed veteran housing placements by addressing costs such as security deposits and application fees or by leasing units directly from property owners.

The foundation is also investing in homelessness prevention and permanent supportive housing through organizations including Operation Homefront and Community Solutions. Additional funding will explore alternative housing approaches, including modular homes from Purple Heart Homes for senior veterans and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

The announcement coincides with the foundation’s annual Celebration of Service. This fall, Team Depot, The Home Depot’s associate volunteer force, is expected to complete hundreds of projects benefiting veterans across all 50 states and three U.S. territories.

One recent project brought The Home Depot Foundation, Team Depot, and Purple Heart Homes together to construct a fully accessible modular home on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., for James “Jim” Taylor, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran who previously experienced homelessness. The home was subsequently transported to Virginia, where a dedication is planned.

#5553. Inside ‘My Big Fat Fabulous Life’ Star Whitney Way Thore’s ‘Dopamine Apartment’

When “My Big Fat Fabulous Life” star Whitney Way Thore moved back to her home state of North Carolina, she fell in love with Jake Beaudoin—and the whimsical Charlotte apartment they now share.

The 42-year-old reality TV personality began renting the “tiny, but enough” one-bedroom, one-bathroom, 830-square-foot unit in December 2025 following her unintentionally brief residency at a New England-style cottage in Salem, MA.

“I love Salem so much, but I had some issues that we didn't really cover in the season, some extended family things. My dad needed a little bit more help at home, so I decided to come on back,” Thore reveals in the latest installment of Celebrity Sanctuary.

Rather than returning to her old stomping ground at the Greensboro, NC, home she still holds or her family’s nearby property, Thore settled into a place inside a “new and modern” building where she could focus on a fresh start with her dog Goosie, cat Wandaleezza Rice, and shortly after her arrival, Beaudoin, now her fiancé.

In an exclusive clip shared with Realtor.com® from the Season 14 premiere of Thore’s TLC series, due to premiere on Nov. 10, Thore unveils her personal pad and its rainbow color palette for the first time while giving her friend and co-star Ashley Baynes a tour.

“I wanted it to be my dopamine apartment. You see how it’s colors, you see how it’s tchotchkes, you see how it’s fun?” asks Thore, as she points out the colorful mod decor she curated for the Queen City dwelling.

While Thore reports Beaudoin was immediately welcoming of the apartment’s playful style, she admits it’s been a challenge to accept his additions since moving in together.

“I don't love his stuff—that's the only issue—but luckily, he's cool with the aesthetic. It fits his vibe,” states Thore.

“It’s been very difficult to have a man in the apartment. ... I made him rent one of the storage units in the apartment for a lot of his stuff. I was basically like, ‘I don't want to see any evidence that you live here,’” she teases. She adds that they have made plans to "move out to a bigger place."

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Thore debuts the cheerfully decorated Charlotte dwelling where she’s found happiness, including the special living room nook she calls the most mood-boosting spot in her home.

When you walk in the door to this apartment, the view of uptown Charlotte through the windows is the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. It is exactly why I picked this apartment.

I feel instantly happy every time I walk in here. This is my favorite place I've ever lived, by miles. I really love what I've done in here.

When I moved to Charlotte, I wanted to feel creative. I was really moving here as a single girly—I didn't think that I was going to be dating anyone—and I wanted to make the space really conducive to feeling stimulated and creative.

I took a lot of liberties in this apartment that I would not do in my family home or in my Greensboro home where I felt like it has to be more grown-up or something like that. I [felt] the freedom to be like, “That's the cutest thing I've ever seen. I'm gonna get that, whether it fits or not.”

It's eclectic. It’s very funky. I have locker cabinets. There's a lot of texture and color, and it feels like motion to me. I have a lot of roundness and waviness: my coffee table, another table, my lamp, my candlesticks—I have a lot of shapes that I wouldn't normally have.

I have a lot of fun, whimsical things in this apartment, and I have a lot of color and a lot of art.

I am obsessed with [Henri] Matisse. I have, like, nine Matisse prints in here, and I even started doing art, which I hadn't done in almost 20 years. That was really exciting for me. I just wanted this space to feel bright and stimulating and exciting.

I have a lot of my own creations in here, things that I've drawn or done. Honestly, the thing I'm most proud of in this apartment is my little basketball gold net chain that I constructed. I got really into basketball when I moved to Charlotte. I started watching the Hornets and I got so into the season.  I don’t consider myself to be very crafty, [but] I ended up making a basketball net with chains and charms and I have that up.

I have a really cool digital picture of my mom that someone on the crew did for me. I have some little things of hers throughout the apartment that make me feel like she's here. I even have some of her handwritten notes on the refrigerator.

Just yesterday I found these glasses [for] $8. They’re like wrought iron. I reorganized ... to make room for the glasses. I'm still constantly picking and refining and moving things, and I'm just such a person that needs to feel so good in my physical space.

My physical space is such a representation of my mental space, so I can't have things super messy. I can't have things out of place.

In terms of the art and the shelving, I put a lot of work into making it fit me and my needs perfectly. I'm so particular and I like things done perfectly, measured perfectly, spaced perfectly.

I have ADHD, so I need little systems exactly how I need them to help me. If there's an extra step, then it's not going to happen.

I have a Russian handyman named Pavel. He is my lifesaver. Pavel and I have spent many, many hours together figuring out just how to make everything exactly how I wanted it, conducive to how I needed things. So no real renovations, but a lot of modifications.

Where I'm sitting right now is what I would consider [my sanctuary]. It's my armchair in the living room. It’s Ikea, so it's probably not real leather, but it's cognac. My rug is a beautiful bright blue; it’s not a pastel. The paint color is a light gray.

I like to read here. I can see straight out the window at night. The skyline and the view is so beautiful and soothing. I see the moon. I see Venus right outside my window. It gives me a peace that I usually experience in nature. I love this little corner where I look out the window, or I can watch TV, or do whatever. I spend a lot of my time out here just sitting.

I actually spend a lot of time in the apartment because I don't have a 9-to-5 job that brings me out of the apartment. That is one of the biggest reasons I've put so much into it and wanted to feel so comfortable in it, because I'm here all the time.

I don't often feel the need to even be out because where I live, you can see the skyline, there's life happening outside everywhere. There's always music, people. There's a train that goes by right outside my window. I feel like I can be in the safety and comfort of my home and still feel like I'm in the world, which is something that I would never have in Greensboro. That's something that I really missed. I felt very isolated and that I had to be out of the house to feel connected to the world. In Charlotte, I feel I'm part of it.

Charlotte really feels good to me. It really feels like home. I don't see myself leaving Charlotte in the next few years at least. I love the neighborhood that I live in. It's the same neighborhood that I lived in pre-COVID and during the beginning of COVID. It's a really wonderful mix of city life, and also, it’s still calm. It’s a really good fit for me and I love it here.

I really do feel like this specific apartment is such a big part of my experience in Charlotte. I'm very attached to it.

#5552. LGI Homes Posts Q3 Gains Despite Slower Sales Activity

LGI Homes posted year-over-year gains in closings, revenue, and earnings during the third quarter, even as affordability pressures continued to weigh on buyer demand and slow sales activity.

The Texas-based builder delivered 1,222 homes during the quarter, up 10.4% from a year earlier, including 33 currently and previously leased homes. Its 1,189 new-home closings generated $437.5 million in home building revenue, an increase of 10.3% year over year. Total revenue increased 10.2% to $444.5 million.

“We delivered strong third quarter financial results, generating year-over-year growth in closings, revenue, and earnings while maintaining strong profitability, expanding our community count, and further strengthening our balance sheet,” chairman and CEO Eric Lipar said.

Net income increased to $24.6 million from $19.7 million in the prior-year quarter, while diluted earnings per share increased to $1.05 from $0.85.

Home building gross margin was 20.2% in the third quarter, while adjusted home building gross margin was 23.7%. Both were above the midpoint of LGI Homes’ previous guidance ranges and improved 40 basis points sequentially.

Lipar attributed the margin performance in part to the company’s predominantly self-developed, on-balance-sheet land position and its approach to balancing affordability and profitability.

“Our teams also did an excellent job managing costs. SG&A expenses declined on an absolute-dollar basis, and SG&A as a percentage of total revenues improved 180 basis points year over year,” he said.

The builder also continued expanding its footprint, ending the third quarter with 151 active communities, an increase of 7.1% from the prior-year period.

Despite stronger closings and revenue, LGI Homes said affordability pressure contributed to slower sales activity during the quarter.

Through the first nine months of 2026, net orders totaled 2,869, compared with 4,098 during the same period in 2025. The cancellation rate increased to 48.9% from 28.1%, while ending backlog declined to 685 homes from 1,305 a year earlier.

The trend marks a reversal from the beginning of the year, when LGI Homes ended the first quarter with 1,699 homes in backlog, up 63.4% year over year. At the time, management pointed to improving sales activity and a growing backlog as evidence of steady demand heading into the spring selling season.

By the third quarter, however, affordability had become a more significant headwind.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership and are leaning into our proven sales and marketing strategies to improve sales pace while maintaining our disciplined approach to balancing affordability and profitability,” Lipar said.

Based on its year-to-date results and current market conditions, LGI Homes narrowed its full-year closing guidance and now expects to deliver between 4,600 and 4,800 homes in 2026. The company said the revised outlook reflects slower sales activity as affordability pressures continue to weigh on demand.

The builder maintained the remainder of its full-year guidance, including an expected average sales price between $360,000 and $370,000 and adjusted home building gross margin between 22.5% and 24.5%.

“As we head into the final quarter of the year, our focus is on finishing 2026 strong,” Lipar said. “Affordability remains the key consideration for today’s buyers, and we have intentionally broadened our sales process to work with more prospective customers who may need additional time to qualify.”

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5551. These Markets Led New-Home Shopper Conversions in Q3

As housing affordability continues to challenge the market and overall shopper activity softens, understanding where prospective buyers are actively engaging becomes increasingly valuable for home building professionals.

Zonda’s latest Homebuyer Outlook shows Houston led major markets for new-home shopper conversions in Q3 2026. Atlanta ranked second, while Riverside rounded out the top three. Atlanta’s performance was particularly notable since the market came in seventh place in Q2 2026.

The results come from Zonda’s proprietary Conversion Index, which gives builders another way to assess buyer interest beyond traffic alone. The index measures the ratio of online shopper clicks to community tour requests on NewHomeSource.com, helping capture the point at which shoppers move beyond researching homes and toward engaging with a community.

While high levels of online shopping can indicate interest in a market, conversions show where consumers are taking a more meaningful action.

That distinction becomes especially useful in a slower demand environment. It also provides another perspective since online shopper activity softened but several markets recorded stronger conversion readings than in the previous quarter. That makes conversion a useful complement to traditional measures of demand.

#5550. IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge join forces to launch quantum computing error-correction platform

IBM Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory today announced a new quantum error-correction platform that integrates quantum and high-performance computing.

Gaining high performance and correctness in quantum computing requires protecting quantum information from noise. In many cases, researchers have paired quantum computers with classical computers to achieve superior performance for running industry-relevant problems. The challenge today is scaling up these advances with classical computing.

Today’s physical quantum qubits make errors roughly once every few hundred operations. Without correction, errors compound rapidly, rendering long or complex calculations completely untenable. Game-changing algorithms such as Shor’s algorithm for factoring or for molecular-scale simulations in chemistry require billions of error-free operations.

This launch uses a co-design platform for quantum error correction using IBM’s quantum computers, including the 120-qubit Nighthawk with ORNL’s Umbra High-Performance Computing system powered by AMD’s Instinct MI355X graphics processing units and 5th Gen EPYC central processing units.

“ORNL’s strength in high-performance computing, combined with the expertise of our QSC partners – like IBM and AMD – creates an opportunity to push the boundaries of what is possible,” said Director of the Quantum Science Center Travis Humble. “With Umbra, we will now test new ideas, evaluate approaches at scale, and build the foundation for more reliable quantum computers.”

Jay Gambetta, an IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research, added that the biggest contributor to today’s research is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware, but how to accelerate and optimize it to build systems scientists can use to tackle problems.

IBM said the Nighthawk’s square-lattice connectivity enables industry-leading speed and real-time control to test error-correction techniques. GPU accelerators, such as AMD’s nodes in the Umbra system, can help with this fine-tuning. The co-design platform connected at Oak Ridge will help explore quantum as part of a broader artificial intelligence and scientific computing infrastructure.

“This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale,” said Gambetta.

Researchers can measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the results in real time, set the exact timing for the signals that protect the qubits from noise, and see exactly what the hardware ran while working with raw measurement signals. This will provide error-correction research with the raw data needed for the next generation of approaches to build sophisticated capabilities for large systems running real code.

Earlier this year, IBM and ORNL unveiled results showing how workloads running on both quantum and classical computers and the Frontier supercomputer can simulate real magnetic materials and calculate molecular configurations of a promising material for fusion fuel.

The simulation of magnetic materials could lead to breakthroughs in superconductors, more efficient batteries and novel drugs. A promising fusion fuel could provide a stepping stone to abundant energy superior to nuclear fission, which powers current nuclear power plants.

#5549. Smith Douglas Homes Grows Q3 Orders and Backlog as Margins Tighten

Smith Douglas Homes continued to grow orders and closings during the third quarter despite mounting affordability pressure. The challenging housing environment weighed heavily on the builder’s profitability.

The No. 33 builder closed 831 homes during the quarter, up 5% from 788 a year earlier. However, home closing revenue increased just 0.2% to $262.5 million as the average sales price of homes closed fell to approximately $316,000 from $333,000 in the prior-year period.

Net new home orders increased 13% to 777 from 690 a year earlier. The contract value of those orders rose to $246.1 million from $231.8 million, while the average sales price of orders declined to approximately $317,000 from $336,000. The quarterly cancellation rate was relatively stable at 11.3%, compared with 11.2% a year earlier.

Backlog increased 25% year over year to 947 homes at the end of September, with a contract value of $305.3 million.

“We continued to execute with discipline during the third quarter despite increasingly challenging housing market conditions,” said CEO and vice chairman Greg Bennett. “Higher mortgage rates and affordability pressures have weighed on buyer demand and profitability, but our teams remain focused on things we can control with respect to managing costs, building efficiently, and maintaining a steady absorption pace.”

While Smith Douglas Homes maintained its sales pace, profitability came under considerably more pressure. Home closing gross margin declined to 16.3% from 21% in the prior-year quarter. Pretax income fell to $3.3 million from $17.2 million, while diluted earnings per share declined to $0.07 from $0.24.

The builder’s lower average selling price highlights the affordability dynamic. The average price of homes closed decreased roughly 5% year over year to $316,000, while the average price of new orders declined about 6% to $317,000.

“While we expect market conditions to remain challenging in the near term, we remain confident in the long-term demand for affordable housing,” Bennett said. “Our priorities continue to be running an efficient home building operation and preserving our financial strength while remaining prepared to take advantage of opportunities as conditions improve.”

Smith Douglas Homes also continued expanding its community footprint during the quarter. The builder ended September with 113 active communities, up 15% from 98 a year earlier. Total controlled lots increased 2% to 24,724, including 22,693 optioned lots.

The company ended the quarter with 1,514 homes under construction, compared to 1,098 last year.

“Our disciplined approach to capital allocation and land investment remains particularly important in today’s operating environment,” said executive vice president and CFO Russ Devendorf. “Our land-light operating model, efficient construction cycle times, and conservative balance sheet provide us with the flexibility to manage through periods of weaker demand without compromising our long-term objectives.”

#5548. Fayetteville’s Growth Continues, but Affordability Is Testing the Market

The Fayetteville metro enters the final months of 2026 with several indicators pointing to continued economic growth. Total households are expected to increase 1.9% year over year to 236,740 in 2026, with annual growth of roughly 2% projected through 2028. Labor market conditions have also remained favorable, as total nonfarm employment grew 3.0% year over year to 311,300 in August and the unemployment rate fell to 3.1%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Several notable projects are moving forward across the region. Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is advancing a nearly $79 million terminal expansion after recording its highest monthly passenger volume on record in July 2026 and surpassing Little Rock in annual enplanements last year. In Bentonville, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine Whole Health Campus recently broke ground, an investment that could help meet rising health care needs as the metro’s 65 and older population continues to grow through 2028.

While demographic indicators and economic activity remain positive, housing market data tells a more mixed story.

Despite continued household and employment growth, home sales activity has slowed. As of July, annualized new home closings totaled 2,033, down 20.4% year over year, compared with an essentially flat decline for annualized existing home closings over the same period.

Pricing remains an important consideration. The median new home closing price reached nearly $380,000 in July, compared with $365,000 for existing homes. Despite that premium, new home demand remains concentrated at more attainable price points. In fact, the largest share of both detached and attached annualized new home closings occurred between $300,000 and $350,000 in July.

Meanwhile, single-family permitting is expected to decline 20.4% year over year in 2026 before decreasing another 15.1% in 2027. What was previously characterized as a housing shortage could become a more competitive environment as supply catches up with demand.

Fayetteville’s important storyline will be turning household and employment growth into qualified housing demand. The fundamentals remain compelling, but affordability and a shifting supply-demand balance are likely to separate the market’s strongest performers from the rest.

#5547. Generational Wealth Fuels Record-High Levels of Cash Sales Among First-Time Buyers

The share of first-time homebuyers paying all cash has climbed to record levels, fueled by generational wealth transfers, even as eroding affordability continues to push homeownership out of reach for many Americans.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 10% of rookie home shoppers paid all cash instead of relying on financing, marking the largest percentage on record, according to the annual Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors®.

The data also reveals that all-cash buyers were roughly three times likelier than financed first-time buyers to have used an inheritance (28% vs. 9%).

Across all first-time buyers—cash or financed—10% used an inheritance toward their home purchase, marking a new record and the fourth straight annual increase.

"The housing market is beginning to see a generational transfer of wealth. It’s not yet a tsunami, but it is changing who can buy a first home and when," says Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research. "Because people are living longer, the generation receiving that wealth isno longer young adults. Many are reaching middle age before they can buy their first home."

In fact, while the median age of first-time buyers held steady at a record high of 40, cash buyers skewed older, with the median age reaching 54 years old, compared to 38 for those who used financing.

Echoing Lautz, Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones confirms that the transfer of wealth from one generation to the next is starting to show up in the housing market, though the full effect won't likely be felt for a few more years.

Older homeowners hold substantial equity, and repeat buyers, with a median age of 62—matching a record high set last year— paid all cash 30% of the time in 2026. Jones says that for some rookie buyers, that wealth arrives as an inheritance.

"Buyers with access to inherited wealth have a significant advantage when they can purchase without financing," Anthony Mian, an agent with Douglas Elliman Beverly Hills, tells Realtor.com. "In multiple-offer situations, sellers often favor all-cash offers because they eliminate financing risk, reduce the likelihood of delays, and provide greater certainty of closing."

Other avenues open to baby boomers wishing to boost their children's or grandchildren's purchasing power include cash gifted toward a down payment, co-signing a loan, or selling investment properties, says Emilee Warner, a real estate agent at MW Real Estate Co. in Nashville, TN.

Looking at the top sources for a down payment among first-time buyers, personal savings continued to dominate (62%), followed by financial assets, such as 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency (30%), and gifts or loans from family and friends (25%).

"Wealth, whether built up or inherited, is increasingly what gets some buyers in, while buyers who depend on a mortgage still face high rates and prices," notes Jones.

Warner says she recently worked with first-time buyers who paid all cash borrowed the "bank" of mom and dad to purchase a home with a price tag exceeding $1 million.

"The cash buyers out there want to get in a home prior to rates dropping," Warner tells Realtor.com. "They are serious, willing, and able buyers. Cash allows appraisals to be waived, removing the risk of a low appraisal that could lose a financed buyer the home."

While more than half of repeat buyers (57%) relied on proceeds from the sale of their previous home and 42% used savings for their down payment, harnessing generational wealth among this cohort is not unheard of, with 4% using an inheritance or a gift from a family member or friend to fund their next home purchase.

Brandon Winn, an agent at Iowa Realty in Des Moines, IA, says he recently worked with move-up buyers who were purchasing a home with the help of their parents who offered them a 3% loan.

"This was when interest rates were 6.5%, and they gave them a 3% loan so they could afford to buy the home that they wanted," Winn tells Realtor.com.

Winn adds that at the luxury tier of the Des Moines market topping $600,000, he is seeing a growing number of buyers paying all cash using either inheritance or investment funds.

"Interest rates have risen so quickly that it's priced a lot of buyers out of the market," says the agent. "So if you have the cash ... it gives you the opportunity to purchase the house without having a [mortgage] payment, and then, of course, you're going to build equity quite a bit faster."

Mian, in Beverly Hills, says that for young families, that additional disposable income can go toward childcare, education, savings, or investments. Access to generational wealth can even expand their housing search geographically.

"In a market as expensive as Los Angeles, this can influence not only who can afford to purchase a home, but also which neighborhoods they can access and how much financial flexibility they retain after purchasing," he says. "Ultimately, generational wealth is becoming an important factor in determining both housing opportunities and long-term financial security."

Affordability continues to be the biggest major hurdle for aspiring U.S. homeowners.

The share of first-time buyers ticked up to 22% from last year's all-time low of 21%, yet it is still roughly half the historical norm of 40% recorded before 2008. Jones attributes the modest year-over-year boost to mortgage rate declines in the beginning of 2026.

Rates briefly dipped below 6% in February, before the outbreak of the Iran war, and were below year-ago levels from October 2025 through July 2026.

"This presented a window of opportunity for first-time buyers relying on a mortgage. The vast majority of first-time buyers financed their purchase, which means the median first-time buyer age is closer to the financed first-time buyer age," says Jones. "All-cash first-time buyers have aged 10 years in a decade, versus six for financed buyers, which shows they are a different group, middle-aged and drawing on savings, investments or inheritance."

Examining the makeup of first-time buyers in 2026, NAR data shows the share of first-time buyers who were married couples decreased slightly to 47%. Single women accounted for a quarter of all first-time buyers, same as in 2025, while the share of single men climbed to 12%, the highest level since 2011.

The typical novice buyer in 2026 had a median household income of $100,000, up from last year's $94,400.

The median down payment among first-time buyers this year was 9%, down from 10% in 2025 and significantly below the 18% recorded among all buyers.

As in years past, equity-rich repeat buyers continued to dominate the market, accounting for 78% of all home purchases with a median household income of $127,000 and a typical down payment of 19%— more than double that of first-timers. Nearly a third (30%) paid all cash.

"Repeat buyers are driving the housing market," says Lautz. "Unlike first-time home buyers, repeat buyers have seen their housing equity grow rapidly over the past decade, enabling them to trade up for larger homes or move into more desirable locations. These are often moves by choice rather than necessity."

The typical home seller in 2026 has owned their property for 12 years, a new all-time high surpassing last year's 11-year tenure. Forty-seven percent of sellers went on to purchase a newer home, and 36% bought a larger home.

Of all homes sold on the market, 78% did not have children under the age of 18 residing in the home, down from 81% last year.

For all sellers, the most commonly cited reason for selling their home was the desire to move closer to friends and family (22%), followed by the home being too small (12%), the home being too large (10%), a change in family situation (8%), and moving due to retirement (8%).

For recently sold homes, the final sales price was a median of 99% of the final listing price.

#5545. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

#5544. Inside Cristiano Ronaldo’s Jaw-Dropping Global Property Portfolio and $1.4 Billion Fortune—as He Retires From International Football

Soccer legend Cristiano Ronaldo has announced his retirement from international football after representing Portugal for 23 years.

"A journey that began in August 2004 and changed my life forever is coming to an end," the soccer icon said in a Nov. 5 Instagram post. "When I look back and think of everything I've experienced with the national team, I don't just see matches, goals, records or trophies. I see people. I see immigrants who, for 90 minutes, felt Portugal was a little bit closer."

For now, Ronaldo will continue to play at the club level with Al-Nassr FC in the Saudi Pro League. His contract extends through June 30, 2027.

The announcement comes months after the whistle was blown on his final World Cup in July. The former Portuguese captain and his team missed out on a spot in the 2026 quarterfinals with a devastating 0-1 loss to Spain in Texas.

Following an incredibly tense and largely goal-less matchup between the two teams, Spain's Mikel Merino managed to slide one past the Portuguese goalie in the 91st minute, cementing his team's place in the quarterfinal game.

Ronaldo, 41, was incredibly emotional as he walked off the pitch—hours after confirming at a press conference that the 2026 FIFA World Cup would be the last he plays in.

Ronaldo—whose country is set to co-host the World Cup in 2030 alongside Spain and Morocco—made the announcement during a July 5 press conference, just one day before Portugal's highly anticipated Round of 16 showdown against Spain in Dallas.

"It's about enjoying it as much as possible. This will be my last World Cup, but let's hope tomorrow isn't my last game," the star athlete said, according to ESPN.

The soccer icon noted that he has a "passion" for football, teasing that he hasn't done "too badly" on the field.

"I don't need it, I have a good life, but it's about passion. I play football because I love it. ... You have to enjoy every day. And I've scored three goals [at this World Cup], I'm not doing too badly, right?" Ronaldo said.

During the 2026 World Cup, Ronaldo became the first player to score in six World Cups when he achieved two goals against Uzbekistan.

Ronaldo marked another career highlight when he scored a penalty against Croatia in the Round of 32, which recorded his first goal in a knockout-round match of a World Cup.

Speaking about this year's tournament, the soccer legend noted, "It's been fantastic. It goes beyond the pitch. ... This is the World Cup I'll remember the most, because of people's passion. It's even more this time, I don't know why. It's been, emotionally, the best. I've enjoyed it very much."

"I'm not lacking anything in life. I'm not going to be more, or less, Cristiano because I win the World Cup. We have the qualities to win, but only one country can win it. ... Age gives you maturity and experience," he said.

Ronaldo has showcased his skills in six World Cup tournaments: 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022, and 2026.

He said that he is grateful for the ups and downs he has experienced throughout that 20-year run, noting that he is even happy to have received public criticism because it has helped him to become a better player.

"I'm thankful even for the attacks I receive, turning 40—and I hope to live another 40 years—with the criticism. That's how you grow the most as a person, and I thank you, journalists, for that," Ronaldo said.

Off the field, Ronaldo has recently entered a new chapter. In August, he married his longtime partner, Georgina Rodriguez in a "private and intimate" ceremony in Portugal. He had proposed in 2025 after eight years of dating.

Ronaldo, who was born and raised in Portugal, began his professional playing career at age 17, when he made his debut for local team Sporting CP. He then moved to the U.K., where he joined Premier League team Manchester United.

During his 23-year career, Ronaldo has become one of the highest-paid soccer players in history, amassing a net worth of $1.4 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. He was, as a result, the first soccer star to become a verified billionaire.

In addition to his very lucrative contracts with some of the world's most elite soccer teams, the player has made an impressive amount of money through endorsement deals representing high-profile brands, including Armani, Nike, and TAG Heuer.

He has also amassed an incredibly impressive property portfolio throughout his career, snapping up homes in his native Portugal, as well as several dwellings farther afield.

Now, as the five-time Ballon d'Or winner calls time on his final FIFA World Cup, attention is once again turning to the legacy he will leave behind—not only through his record-breaking career, but also through an enviable collection of multimillion-dollar homes stretching from Portugal to Saudi Arabia.

Ronaldo first picked up a property in Portugal's capital in 2015 for $2 million.

The dwelling is located on Avenida da Liberdade, a boulevard that is inspired by Paris' Champs-Elysees and is adorned with boutiques, hotels, and cafes.

In 2018, he purchased a 3,100-square-foot-penthouse for $7 million, making history with the then-most expensive apartment ever sold in the city.

The property boasts three bedrooms, wood floors, a terrace, and glass walls that allow natural light to flood inside.

The home also features a spa, gym, and resort-style pool.

From 2009 to 2018, Ronaldo played for Real Madrid and sealed his legacy when he became the club's all-time leading scorer.

In 2010, the soccer star snapped up a luxe mansion in the La Finca neighborhood, a gated community known for its celebrity residents and 24/7 security.

The property, which was designed by Joaquín Torres, sprawls across 8,600 square feet.

It comes complete with a spa, cyrochamber, indoor pool, and even a soccer field.

In 2023, he placed the property on the market for rent for about $11,000 a month.

Ronaldo also made sure to pick up a property where he grew up—in Madeira, Portugal.

He splashed out $8 million for the seven-story abode, which was transformed from a former nightclub in 2015.

The dwelling boasts a rooftop pool, two gyms, and an indoor pool.

Although Ronaldo isn't always able to make it there, his mother and brother reportedly reside there full time.

By 2018, the soccer star picked up another pad in one of Turin's most lavish communities: Strada San Vito Revigliasco.

Inside, the home boasts chic marble, a spa, a gym and several resort-style pools.

After picking up a property in Turin, Ronaldo took a vacation to Marbella, Spain, and decided that he needed a getaway in the area.

The $1.6 million dwelling is situated in the development known as "Superstars' Cul-de-Sac."

The area is famous for its celebrity residents, including Conor McGregor, and offers panoramic views of the Mediterranean and several golfing areas.

His holiday home features four bedrooms, high ceilings, glass walls, a pool, a gym, a wine cellar, and a lavish home theater.

Elsewhere in Portugal, Ronaldo purchased a 2.47-acre plot built in the lavish Quinta da Marinh for $30 million.

The sprawling property was built between 2022 and 2023.

It comes complete with a home theater, spa, tennis court, two pools, and 30-car garage.

In 2022, the pro athlete moved to Riyadh to join Saudi Arabian team Al-Nassr—initially relocating to the Kingdom Centre Hotel, where he and his family lived for an entire month before settling down at a full-time residence.

That property is located in Al-Muhammadiyah, one of Riyadh’s most exclusive enclaves.

His home reportedly boasts modern lighting, a three-car garage, a lavish pool, and a luxe walk-in closet.

In 2024, Ronaldo picked up a home in Dubai's Jumeirah Bay Island, also known as "Billionaires Island."

The waterfront mansion is situated in a man-made enclave that can be accessed only by a private bridge.

#5542. Exclusive: StrongestLayer launches tools to verify payment requests and block hidden AI instructions

Artificial intelligence email security startup StrongestLayer Inc. today launched two products aimed at email that can move money or manipulate an AI assistant.

The first product, Intent Workflows, can hold payment, payroll and executive account requests for verification before anyone acts on them. Alongside it comes AI Instruction Intercept, which stops hidden instructions in a message before an assistant such as Microsoft Corp.’s Microsoft 365 Copilot reads them

Intent Workflows targets attacks that carry no malware or suspicious link. In vendor email compromise, a criminal takes over a real supplier’s mailbox and sends new bank details inside an existing thread.

StrongestLayer went through 32,052 attacks that got past existing defenses at 45 organizations in the second quarter. Only 3.6% were payment or bank-change requests. Under a loss model built on the Factor Analysis of Information Risk framework, that small slice accounted for more than 98% of the estimated financial exposure. Sender authentication checks were little help, since 94% of those messages passed them.

Traditional email security asks whether a message looks bad, according to Alan LeFort, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief executive. “The costliest attacks are built to look fine,” he said. His company looks at what a message is trying to make happen, which for a wire transfer means “verifying the action instead of betting on a verdict.”

StrongestLayer’s detection still screens every message. Intent Workflows adds a hold for the smaller set of requests that can’t be reversed, with each customer deciding whether those requests wait for verification or go to the security team or a process owner.

Customers can also let a request through with a policy banner, which appears only on tracked requests and spells out the company’s own rule, such as “Bank change: call the number on file.” Payments in scope are held whatever the verdict, so a hijacked vendor account can’t get one through by sounding legitimate.

The software compares each payment request with the payee’s history, and customers pick the threshold, whether that is every payment or only those over $5,000. If nothing has changed, the payment owner confirms in one click, in Microsoft Teams or by email. Any change, or a new vendor, means a call to a phone number already on file, and the email isn’t released until the outcome is logged.

Payroll changes are verified the same way, and executive password, multifactor authentication and account recovery resets go to the identity or security team first, even when the request comes in through the help desk.

The release also takes on a newer problem. Researchers at Aim Security Ltd. found the EchoLeak flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot last year, and one crafted email was all it took to get the assistant leaking data.

AI Instruction Intercept reads each message first. A reasoning model checks it for hidden instructions against the customer’s own business context, and only after that does the email reach Copilot, Google LLC’s Gemini or a security classifier. Suspect messages are quarantined by default with an explanation of what each instruction was after.

Email is the one route to an AI assistant that “any outsider can use,” said Joshua Bass, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief product officer. He argues the inbox is the first place to stop prompt injection, since all an attacker needs is an address.

Both products are available now for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace and run alongside a company’s existing email security.
