#5476. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5475. Can the new Congress help lower mortgage rates?

After a Democratic midterm win, lawmakers may try to ease drivers of inflation tied to oil, AI investment, tariffs, and jobs. The Fed is likely to respond mainly through how these factors move the 10-year yield and inflation expectations.  AI Summary

After the Democrats’ historic midterm win, the question now is: can the new Congress help get mortgage rates lower? Obviously, the Iran conflict and trade war have taken their toll on President Trump’s approval ratings, but can Congress — both Democrats and Republicans — now work together on getting something done that the President will not veto?

Let’s look at the economic factors influencing rates in this environment, what Congress can do about each, and how the Fed might consider these as they set monetary policy.

When WTI oil was at $112 on April 7 this year, the 10-year yield was at 4.31% — but back then the Fed was still talking about cutting rates two to three times. A lot has changed since then.The Federal Reserve has made the Iran conflict a big talking point, so some type of resolution to this conflict could impact rates. Obviously, the conflict has hurt President Trump and the Republicans; it’s very unpopular, especially with farmers and truckers who have to deal with high diesel prices. Trump himself acknowledged the war played a major part in the midterm results.

Congress made some attempts to try to end this conflict in the past, but may have renewed incentives now to find a solution. We shall see what comes next, as President Trump has said he could make a deal after the midterms.

Now, the AI boom is a little bit more complicated because there are a lot of projects still in the pipeline that can’t be shut down by the Democrats right now, but future projects could definitely be affected. And with some type of regulation and moratorium, some of the growth prospects might be slowed down.

This is a critical factor because the Federal Reserve has really made the AI boom and inflation a hot topic. It’s part of the reason why, when you see AI softness — whether it’s the credit markets or their stock prices getting hit — bond traders tend to want to buy bonds, not sell them, in that environment. For now, the Fed needs to see a material slowdown to lose its hawkish stance on AI, but it would be another positive for rates.

On another note, the labor productivity data was awesome today. This data really affects how the Fed sees AI and will be the best news for mortgage rates if this trend continues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh himself has made a dovish case around AI as long as it creates more productivity and lowers labor unit costs.

Here is the chart of the 10-year yield for the last six months as of this second, the 10-year yield is down once again to 4.83% as AI stocks are selling off.

This will be very interesting because I am sure President Trump will try every legal angle to continue his tariff policy — he still wants to have tariffs because it’s his favorite tool to cut deals. However, what the midterms have done is limit the power he can have to escalate the trade war into something worse. That can be a very big positive: we might have seen the high of the 10-year yield at 5.35% if the trade war doesn’t get worse amid the conflict with Iran.

For now, we need to wait and see how much farther the President wants to push the trade war. He might just cut a deal with Canada, leave other countries alone and just focus on China — which would be a positive for rates.

Usually, in an economic cycle, when manufacturing jobs and construction jobs are being lost, it’s not a good sign for the labor market: we saw that in 2025. But the labor market has improved this year and that has kept the Fed’s focus fully on inflation.

One thing to think about going forward is that, if we do have some data center moratoriums and rates stay elevated, construction labor might get hit a little bit harder than before the midterms. If the unemployment rate rises as growth slows down, that will be a positive for mortgage rates.

For rates to really make a meaningful move lower and stick, three of the four things above need to get better. You need to get oil prices trading between $67 and $82. You need to get diesel prices down so the Fed won’t talk about energy prices being passed onto the consumer. You’ve got to de-escalate the trade war 2.0 and get some deals in and not make it inflationary.

The AI moratorium and regulations will be a welcome signal to the Federal Reserve; whether that impacts the construction data enough to matter to them is still an open question, but the three things above need to occur to have rates go under 7% and stay there.

#5473. Secure borders. A stronger economy. Washington must deliver both

The editorial calls for immigration enforcement that protects due process and lawful work, plus modernized pathways aligned to construction labor needs. It points to Harvard and NAHB data and urges homebuilding leaders to press for measurable policy outcomes on affordability and productivity.  AI Summary

In the first 100 days of the Trump administration, business leaders at residential construction and development companies were, in effect, summoned to the nation’s capital for an all-hands meeting with administration officials on housing affordability. The summons came on short notice, on a Sunday afternoon. The invitation carried an undertone. Attend or else.

The Washington, D.C., meeting never took place. But the episode captured the breakneck pace and take-no-prisoners approach of those early, flood-the-zone months. It also dialed in a distinctly unsettling tone for the rules of engagement between the new administration and the nation’s private-sector business leaders in one of the economy’s critical engines: homebuilding.

Now, following the 2026 midterm elections, those rules of engagement stand an opportunity to change.

Business leaders, including corporate strategists and their representatives on Capitol Hill, have a window to act quickly, elevate their priorities, and press for policy changes that have damaged or threaten to undermine some of the nation’s most important economic capabilities.

For homebuilding, residential development, and residential investment, immigration enforcement belongs near the top of the agenda.

The United States needs secure borders and enforceable immigration laws. It also needs the workforce capacity to build homes, grow food, manufacture products, and sustain economic growth. These are not competing national interests, and treating them as such has real economic consequences.

The question for President Trump, the incoming Congress, and the business leaders with a stake in the outcome is whether the next two years can achieve a more rational, workable balance among those objectives.

For the housing industry, evidence of what’s at risk is already accumulating.

Over recent months, HousingWire TBD has documented the increasingly disruptive effects of immigration enforcement on residential construction businesses and their trade partners.

Builders and contractors report job site interruptions, workers reluctant to report for work, and crews disappearing from construction schedules. In some affected markets, executives have reported reductions of 60% to 80% in available trade crews. These are accounts from specific businesses and markets, not nationwide estimates.

The disruption also extends beyond workers who lack legal authorization. Reports that U.S. citizens and legally authorized workers are apprehensive about reporting to job sites suggest that enforcement-related fear can diminish workforce availability and productivity.

Residential construction depends on the coordinated sequencing of specialized trades. When a framing crew is unavailable, subsequent work may be delayed, schedules are extended, financing costs accumulate, and closings slip.

For builders and their trade partners operating with already compressed margins and limited capital flexibility, repeated disruptions can pose a serious business risk.

These accounts do not establish that immigration enforcement has caused a nationwide construction crisis. They do, however, raise a question policymakers cannot responsibly ignore: Are enforcement practices achieving legitimate security objectives while imposing avoidable economic costs on lawful workers, responsible employers, and American households?

A study published on October 8 by Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that foreign-born workers accounted for 35% of the nation’s construction trades workforce in 2024, compared with 18% of the overall U.S. labor force.

Their representation is especially high in trades critical to home completion: 57% of drywall and ceiling-tile installers, 53% of roofers and painters, and 51% of flooring installers were foreign-born.

Harvard’s research found that foreign-born workers accounted for all net growth in the construction trades workforce from 2013 to 2024.

Separate NAHB research found that Hispanic workers represented 32.8% of the construction workforce in 2024, up from 23.6% in 2010. In Texas and California, approximately six in 10 construction workers are Hispanic.

Foreign-born status, Hispanic ethnicity, citizenship, and legal employment authorization are distinct characteristics. These statistics cannot be used interchangeably to describe immigration status. Nor do they, nor can they, truly reflect the full impact of foreign-born workers on job site capability and productivity because many undocumented frontline crew members are not counted at all.

The statistics, however, illustrate the industry’s substantial dependence on a diverse workforce, whose lawful participation must be protected.

Meanwhile, labor shortages are worsening despite reduced housing production. NAHB’s September 2026 survey found that, averaged across nine consistently tracked trades, 47% of builders reported labor shortages, up from 42% in April 2025. Framing shortages reached 57%, while finished carpentry shortages reached 58%.

NAHB also identified immigration-enforcement-related worker apprehensions as a contributor to worsening shortages, along with competition from other construction sectors.

Immigration enforcement did not create the industry’s longstanding workforce problems. Those problems reflect decades of insufficient domestic workforce development, shifting demographics, competition for skilled labor, and limited productivity gains. But making an already constrained workforce even less available cannot be a rational part of a national housing affordability strategy.

Washington does not need to start from scratch.

Bipartisan immigration reform initiatives have repeatedly recognized the need to combine effective border security, lawful employment pathways, immigration-system modernization, and solutions for established workers and employers.

NAHB’s comprehensive immigration reform policy, updated in November 2025, provides a practical foundation for the industry. It supports border security and effective enforcement, along with construction-specific visa reforms, legal workforce pathways, and domestic workforce development.

The association has also endorsed the bipartisan DIGNITY Act, which would strengthen border security while establishing conditional pathways to lawful employment for certain undocumented workers who meet defined requirements.

These proposals involve difficult choices and legitimate disagreements. They show that practical approaches exist beyond the familiar binary choice between unrestricted enforcement and abandoning enforcement altogether.

The remaining weeks of the current Congress and the next two years should be evaluated against three governing objectives.

First, the administration must enforce immigration laws while protecting lawful employment and upholding due process. Enforcement priorities, worker-identification procedures, and accountability mechanisms should minimize unnecessary disruption to legitimate businesses and protect citizens and authorized workers from improper detention or interference.

Second, Congress and the administration must develop lawful workforce pathways that reflect documented economic needs. That means considering construction-specific employment programs, modernizing immigration processing, and addressing established workers’ circumstances through clear eligibility, screening, compliance, and worker-protection requirements.

Third, immigration policymaking must elevate economic productivity and affordability as measurable priorities. Congress should assess workforce availability, construction delays, business costs and housing production alongside border-security and enforcement outcomes.

None of these objectives diminishes employers’ obligation to comply with the law, protect workers, invest in apprenticeships and technical education, or to improve productivity through innovation.

America needs stronger domestic workforce development and a workable immigration policy, not one in place of the other.

The industry’s responsibility cannot end with documenting the disruption and asking Washington for relief. Homebuilders, residential developers, investors, building-products manufacturers, trade contractors, and their associations have the evidence, economic standing, and organizational capacity to demand a coherent policy response.

NAHB has already established a reform framework and identified legislative priorities. Industry executives have documented the operational consequences, and research institutions have quantified the workforce’s dependence on immigration.

What, then, are business leaders waiting for?

The next step should be a coordinated, industry-wide agenda presented to the administration and congressional leadership, including specific legislative priorities, credible evidence of business impacts, and commitments to lawful employment, investment in the domestic workforce, and improved productivity.

Not another statement of concern. Not another round of partisan accusations. A sustained effort to translate widely acknowledged economic needs into workable policy.

The new political balance in Washington creates an opening, but divided government does not automatically lead to better governance. Progress will require leaders willing to negotiate, make difficult choices, and accept accountability for results.

The homebuilding industry should not passively wait to see whether that happens. Its leaders have both a direct business interest and a broader responsibility to help make it possible.

America should not have to choose between secure borders and a productive economy. President Trump and Congress should be held accountable for delivering on both fronts.

Not only should the homebuilding industry insist that it do so, but the industry’s leaders should strike with the same speed and ferocity the Administration used to kick-start its agenda almost two years ago.

Donald Trump crypto empire faces fresh pressure as Republicans lose control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, handing Democrats a sweeping victory. The political setback comes as Trump-linked tokens remain deeply underwater and Justin Sun escalates his legal fight against World Liberty Financial, the WLFI.

Sun is seeking nearly $264,000 in sanctions over alleged failures to disclose the project’s UAE ownership ties, and the midterm defeat gives Democrats greater power to investigate Trump’s administration and scrutinize potential conflicts of interest involving his family’s business interests.

Meanwhile, the market has delivered its own verdict. Official Trump, Melania Meme and WLFI tokens have fallen sharply from their peaks, leaving investors nursing substantial losses.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The latest legal pressure comes from Justin Sun, who invested $45 million in WLFI tokens before his relationship with the Trump-backed crypto project deteriorated.

Sun sued World Liberty Financial in April, accusing the company of fraud and unlawfully freezing his tokens. The project later countersued, describing his claims as a “meritless PR stunt.”

Now, the Justin Sun dispute has escalated into a fight over WLFI’s corporate ownership disclosures. Sun alleges World Liberty initially identified Florida as its sole citizenship in federal court. Months later, the company amended its filing to identify 22 entities in its ownership chain, claiming citizenship across Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the United Arab Emirates.

Last night, my lawyers moved to sanction World Liberty Financial @worldlibertyfi for failing to disclose, until months into my litigation against the company, that it is a citizen of the UAE 🇦🇪 . #WLFI #USD1 For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s…

The amended disclosure came shortly after an August hearing addressing World Liberty’s attempt to move parts of the dispute into arbitration. The legal dispute arrives as Trump-linked digital assets remain far below their launch-era highs. The official Trump crypto token reached $73.43 in January 2025 before falling to around $1.50. That leaves TRUMP down 98% from its peak.

Melania Meme, the first lady of America-tied meme coin, has suffered an even steeper decline. The token previously reached approximately $13.05 but has since traded near seven cents, representing a loss exceeding 99%.

WLFI has also retreated from its all-time high near $0.33 to roughly five cents. Its fully diluted valuation remains substantial, but its market price reflects a sharp reversal from launch expectations.

The downturn has left Trump crypto investors facing losses while the project’s political and legal connections draw renewed attention.

World Liberty also operates USD1, its dollar-pegged stablecoin, which has grown into a major part of the project’s business. The company’s financial and ownership structure could receive greater scrutiny as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

The midterm results have not triggered investigations into Trump crypto ventures, but Democrats will gain subpoena power and greater influence over congressional oversight once the new Congress convenes.

The Trump crypto story is no longer just about political branding and token launches. It is increasingly about investor losses, corporate transparency, and the legal consequences of operating a business tied to the presidency.

#5471. Humanoid robot maker Agility Robotics debuts on the Nasdaq after SPAC merger

Agility Robotics Inc. debuted on the Nasdaq today after merging with a special-purpose acquisition company.

SPAC deals provide a simpler path to public markets than a traditional listing. In such transactions, a shell company floats its shares and then merges with a privately held business. That business effectively takes the SPAC’s place on the stock exchange where it’s listed.

Agility merged with an investment vehicle called Churchill Capital Corp XI Corp. on Wednesday. The deal and certain “related financings” together pulled in $465 million, a sum that excludes transaction fees. Agility will use the capital to bring its latest Digit 5 robot to market and add manufacturing capacity.

Digit 5 (pictured) is a nearly six-foot-tall humanoid robot with a 20-hour battery life. It moves using custom actuators based on so-called cycloidal drive technology. That’s a motor design that trades off some speed for increased lifting power: Agility says that the Digit 5 can carry up to 50 pounds at a time.

The robot’s batteries are made by a British startup called Nyobolt Ltd. They use niobium, a metal most commonly found in superconductors and jewelry, to speed up charging. Agility says that the Digit 5 can be recharged in just nine minutes, a fraction of the time required by earlier technologies.

The robot runs some of its software on Nvidia’s IGX Thor system-on-chip series. The most advanced chip in the lineup, the T7000, combines a 14-core central processing unit with a computer vision accelerator and two graphics processing units. One is an embedded GPU with 2,560 cores while the other is a standalone chip originally designed for workstations.

Digit 5 also makes use of Nvidia’s HALOS software toolkit. The suite includes algorithms that help robots avoid hazards. Additionally, HALOS provides resources that make it easier to secure the safety certifications required for commercial deployment.

Agility says that it has received more than $300 million worth of pre-orders for Digit 5. Its customers include Toyota Motor Co. and GXO Logistics Inc., a publicly traded transportation company. Agility claims that it also has three other large customers in the manufacturing sector along with a pipeline of more than 30 prospects.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Agility Chief Executive Officer Peggy Johnson. “Becoming a public company gives us access to more resources to help accelerate that progress, bring intelligent robots to more workplaces and help build a future where people and robots accomplish more together.”

Agility plans to make Digit 5 available through an early access program in the first half of 2027. General availability is slated for later that year. The company will manufacture Digit 5 at a  70,000-square-foot factory in Salem, Oregon with planned capacity of up to 10,000 robots per year.

#5470. Rice breaks ground on the Arc in the Ion District, expanding Houston's innovation ecosystem

Nearly 200,000-square-foot research hub will connect Rice, industry and entrepreneurs to accelerate discovery, collaboration and commercialization

HOUSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rice University broke ground on the Arc in the Ion District, a nearly 200,000-square-foot research, corporate innovation and office building designed to bring researchers, industry leaders, entrepreneurs, investors and top talent together to accelerate innovation and move ideas from discovery to real-world application.

Located in Houston's Ion District powered by Rice, the Arc will feature seven floors of flexible, future-ready lab and office space for Rice and other organizations seeking proximity to leading research, highly skilled workers and Houston's dynamic innovation ecosystem. Rice will be a lead tenant, occupying nearly 80,000 square feet, or about 40% of the building.

"The Arc is a significant investment in Rice's future and in Houston's continued growth as a center for innovation," said Robert T. Ladd, chairman of the Rice Board of Trustees. "It will create new opportunities for industry leaders, researchers and students to work together on ideas with the potential for lasting impact."

The Arc will share a plaza with the Ion building, extending the 12-block Ion District and placing researchers in close proximity to companies, startups, investors and entrepreneurs.

"The Arc will bring Rice's extraordinary research and talent and Houston's impactful innovation ecosystem into even closer connection with the industries and innovators working to solve some of the world's most consequential challenges," said Rice President Reginald DesRoches. "That constant exchange of ideas and expertise will help move discoveries more rapidly from the laboratory to real-world impact."

Built for advanced research and collaboration

The facility will offer flexible lab and office environments that can adapt to evolving research and business needs. Floor plates will range from 28,000 to 31,000 square feet, with 15-foot floor-to-floor heights and infrastructure capable of supporting advanced HVAC, high-capacity electrical and emergency power systems and core laboratory requirements.

The building will also include conference and meeting spaces, an amenity lounge, fitness center, outdoor plazas, underground parking, secure bike storage and on-site retail and dining â creating opportunities to build solutions in the lab, develop partnerships across the district and connect informally throughout the day. The project is designed to meet LEED Gold criteria and will incorporate smart-building and energy-saving features.

"We are creating more than a high-performance business and research building," said Kelly Fox, Rice executive vice president for operations, finance and support. "The Arc is being designed as a destination where companies can access sophisticated infrastructure, connect with one another and build the relationships that lead to new ideas and opportunities."

Work within the building will span areas including artificial intelligence and machine learning, data science, robotics, quantum science and engineering, energy and more.

The groundbreaking event comes on the heels of the university's recent announcement of a transformational universitywide AI initiative to recruit 75 faculty members working across disciplines and expand AI-related courses and degrees. The initiative is accelerating Rice's emergence as a global leader in advanced computing and responsible AI.

"The closer researchers are to the people confronting real-world problems, the more opportunities there are to identify important questions, test ideas and improve solutions," said David Sholl, Rice executive vice president for research. "The Arc gives us an environment built specifically for that kind of sustained collaboration."

Rice's new AI Foundry will be located inside the Arc, where faculty AI experts will have offices and work with industry partners to tackle complex challenges, rapidly develop practical solutions and help organizations build long-term AI capabilities.

The effort will address a growing challenge: AI is advancing faster than many traditional industry innovation models can adapt. Instead of relying on lengthy, linear development cycles, the Foundry will bring Rice experts and industry partners together to identify high-value opportunities, design and test solutions, deploy them in real-world settings and continually refine them based on results.

The Foundry is envisioned to support organizations through AI readiness assessments, feasibility studies, proofs of concept, deployment-ready solutions, executive education and customized workforce training.

"The AI Foundry is exactly the kind of collaboration the Arc is designed to enable," said Amy Dittmar, the Howard R. Hughes Provost and executive vice president for academic affairs. "By bringing Rice researchers together with industry partners in a shared environment, we can accelerate the movement of ideas from research into practical applications while helping organizations build the capabilities they need to succeed as AI continues to evolve."

Responsible AI is a key catalyst in Momentous: Personalized Scale for Global Impact, Rice's strategic plan, which also calls for strategic faculty growth and specifically identifies cross-disciplinary cluster hiring as a way to build depth and breadth in areas vital to the university's future. The institution's four AI cluster areas are foundational AI; two applied areas including AI for health and AI for energy, the environment and resiliency; and responsible AI: society and ethics.

The Arc will complement the Ion building, the namesake centerpiece of Houston's innovation corridor and home to corporate and industry partners including Chevron, Microsoft, Aramco, ExxonMobil, Oxy, Shell, United, Transocean and Woodside Energy.

Co-working space in the Ion managed by Industrious is fully occupied, with more than 250 member companies. Activate, an organization that scientists and engineers become founders and move research toward commercialization, recently launched its third cohort of fellows. Twenty-five startups have participated in the program to date.

Companies based in the Ion, including Persona AI, CES Renewable, Greenflash Infrastructure and Cognite, also have experienced significant growth, reinforcing the building's role as a home for emerging companies and technology-driven organizations. The Ion's development also extends beyond offices and laboratories. MADabolic, a strength-training gym, recently opened in the building. Greentown Labs, Community Artists' Collective and Pickle Lab are also among the organizations that call the district home.

Together, the Ion and the Arc are intended to create a more connected environment where researchers, entrepreneurs, established companies and the broader Houston community can work, meet and exchange ideas.

"Houston has an extraordinary concentration of industry expertise, capital, talent and entrepreneurial energy," said Bobby Tudor, Rice alumnus and chairman of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative. "The Arc will help turn that concentration into action by creating more opportunities for breakthrough research to become technologies and companies."

The project is being developed by Rice Real Estate Co. Construction is expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2028. Preleasing opportunities are now open for companies and organizations interested in locating alongside Rice researchers and joining the broader Ion District ecosystem.

For more information, visit https://www.thearciondistrict.com/.

About Rice UniversityLocated on a 300-acre forested campus in Houston, Texas, Rice University is consistently ranked among the nation's top 20 universities by U.S. News & World Report. Rice has highly respected schools of architecture, business, continuing studies, engineering and computing, humanities and arts, music, natural sciences and social sciences and is home to the Baker Institute for Public Policy and Kinder Institute for Urban Research. Internationally, the university maintains the Rice Global Paris Center, a hub for innovative collaboration, research and inspired teaching located in the heart of Paris, and Rice Global India in Bengaluru, India. With 4,793 undergraduates and 4,185 graduate students, Rice's undergraduate student-to-faculty ratio is just under 6-to-1. Its residential college system builds close-knit communities and lifelong friendships, just one reason why Rice is ranked in the top 10 for best quality of life by the Princeton Review.

#5469. NYC pied-a-terre tax notices get an appeals court green light

A state appeals court dismissed a homeowners’ lawsuit that had disrupted NYC’s pied-a-terre tax notice rollout, finding no standing or injury. A separate challenge by Steve Wynn and Wilbur Ross to the underlying state law remains pending.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration won another round on the pied-à-terre tax Wednesday, when a state appeals court dismissed a homeowners’ lawsuit that had upended the surcharge’s rollout.

Appeals judges threw out an earlier Staten Island judge’s ruling ordering the city to cancel about 17,000 notices. They found the homeowners lacked standing and weren’t injured by the notices. All four judges agreed.

The surcharge is a pillar in the city’s plan to close a $12 billion budget gap. State officials projected it would raise about $500 million a year. The comptroller estimates the impact at closer to $1 billion before exemptions and appeals.

Wednesday’s decision does not directly affect a separate suit by billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn, former Trump administration Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and his wife. They have challenged the state law behind the tax. That case remains pending in Suffolk County, with hearings scheduled in December.

A Staten Island judge had ruled Sept. 29 that the city skipped individualized decisions before mailing notices. The judge called the notices arbitrary and capricious and a due process violation.

Under the order, the Department of Finance was to cancel the notices and pull its roll from the agency website. New notices were allowed after an individualized review. Within hours, the city appealed and invoked a stay, so implementation continued.

Residential brokers told HousingWire TBD that the legal back-and-forth and the tax itself have had little impact on the owner-occupied market.

Ian Slater, co-founder and CEO of Trove Partners, said the market for under $5 million slowed in September and October. “We hit a record number of contract signatures above $5 million in September and October,” he said.

Wealth from a soaring stock market, plus nerves about its froth, is pushing buyers into top-end property, Slater said. Those buyers are “fully ignoring the pied-à-terre tax.” Some want second homes in New York City, he said.

However, listings of such properties remain scarce. Jessica Chestler, co-founder of The Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman, said bidding wars have erupted. Supply isn’t keeping pace with buyer demand, including for homes priced above $5 million.

“We recently represented a buyer in a bidding war that we ultimately won, but it required going $1 million over asking on an apartment that needed a complete gut renovation,” Chestler said.

Because the homeowners lacked standing, the court never ruled on whether the NYC Department of Finance’s rollout was lawful. The court said other arguments were either without merit or unnecessary to resolve.

Finance later used 2025 tax data to revise its determinations, the court noted. Several hundred owners learned they did not owe the surcharge. The surcharge covers only non-primary residences. Through July 2028, the measure impacts houses worth $5 million or more. Co-ops and condos face a $1 million threshold.

Wynn and the Rosses sued in late September. They argue the surcharge is an illegal property tax that discriminates against nonresidents. Wynn’s notice totaled $183,094.69, while the Rosses’ notice came to $83,531.52.

Trove Partners’ Slater does not expect the climate to change. “Political winds are clearly against the wealthy class,” he said.

He doubts judges or politicians will move away from the tax. “It’s definitely an annoyance, but it’s a bit of much ado about nothing,” he said.

#5467. American Housing Corp names leadership for new Austin division

American Housing Corporation launched in Austin with a focus on infill urban rowhomes. The company completed a “Demo 2” prototype using a componentized prefab system and is building a 250,000-square-foot Southeast Austin plant to produce up to 1,200 homes a year.  AI Summary

The American Housing Corporation launched an Austin homebuilding division and named three industry veterans to lead the new operation as it ramps up an infill-focused, prefabricated rowhome platform, the company announced this week.

Austin is the launch market for the company’s infill homebuilding strategy, which centers on designing, manufacturing and constructing urban rowhomes. The move comes as builders look for ways to add “missing middle” housing in supply-constrained, high-cost markets without relying solely on traditional greenfield development.

Parker Scott, a former division president at LGI Homes, was appointed general manager, Daniel Green will serve as director of construction operations and Luke Allen will serve as director of land.

Scott brings more than 20 years of homebuilding sales and operational experience to the role. Green joins from senior construction positions at Homebound, ATCO Structures and Perry Homes, where he focused on building operations and execution systems. Allen, who previously held land roles at Lennar and Ashton Woods, will oversee land acquisition, underwriting and pipeline development for the Austin market.

In October 2026, American Housing Corp completed its “Demo 2” prototype using a componentized, prefabricated building system. The company is building a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant in Southeast Austin designed to produce up to 1,200 homes annually, according to the announcement.

The factory-scale approach is intended to standardize production, shorten build times and provide more cost certainty, which could appeal to capital providers and municipalities looking for scalable infill housing solutions. For real estate investors and lenders, the combination of an infill land strategy with a controlled-offsite construction environment could change underwriting assumptions around cycle times and construction risk.

Alongside the Austin division launch, the company restructured its real estate operations and parted ways with co-founder Bobby Fijan. The firm credited Fijan with helping establish its early real estate footprint and championing urban, family-sized housing.

#5466. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

#5464. RealPRO Select helps lift Realtor.com revenue

Realtor.com reported $160 million in fiscal Q1 2027 revenue, up 5% year over year, extending an eight-quarter growth streak. News Corp cited RealPRO Select expansion and broader RealAssist AI rollout as key drivers.  AI Summary

Move, the parent company of Realtor.com, said the momentum generated by RealPRO Select in fiscal year 2026 has carried over into the first quarter of fiscal year 2027.

During the first quarter of FY 2027, Realtor.com recorded $160 million in revenue, up 5% year over year, marking the segment’s eighth consecutive quarter of growth. These financial results were highlighted during News Corp’s fiscal year 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday evening.

“In a housing market constrained by 7%-plus mortgage rates, Damian [Eales] and the team have exhibited exceptional discipline in their operational focus and AI integration, and that approach has converted revenue growth into meaningful bottom-line expansion,” Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, said during the earnings call.

News Corp executives attributed Realtor.com’s strong revenue performance to the growth of RealPRO Select. The company said it is focused on enhancing the platform with stronger lead generation, branding, productivity tools and training capabilities.

Realtor.com also focused on the expansion of RealAssist AI during Q1, including the launch of a pilot of RealAssist in Rich Communication Services (RCS), integrated directly into Google search and available on iOS and Android.

“The pilot is already attracting new users, driving strong engagement, and helping us capture pre-search intent earlier in the buyer journey before consumers ever enter a browser,” Damian Eales, the CEO of Move, wrote in a blog post about the company’s quarterly performance.

In addition, Realtor.com also launched RealAssist AI for Realtor.com+, which Eales said helps agents onboard their clients faster, build more tailored searches, summarize client activity and draft follow-ups in their own voice.

“The platform is already supporting thousands of successful agent-client connections, and early feedback on these AI tools has been very positive,” Eales wrote.

Eales also highlighted the relaunch of the My Home dashboard, which now includes a collaboration with Opendoor. Eales said this is encouraging sellers to engage a listing agent much earlier in their journey.

In addition, News Corp also noted that Comscore data shows 4.9 visits per unique user to Realtor.com, up 8% annually, and an average of 263 million monthly visits in the quarter, which the company said represents a “substantial” lead over Redfin and Homes.com.

Despite these strong numbers, Realtor.com noted that lead volume was down 11%, which the portal attributed to broader market conditions and its repositioning of customer acquisitions to higher-quality and higher-value leads.

“Despite a constrained housing market, Realtor.com’s strategy is delivering positive results, and we’re well positioned to grow as conditions improve,” Eales wrote. “Our focus remains on investing in our audience and AI tools that enhance a consumer’s experience and augment the role of the professional agent.”

Overall, News Corp’s digital real estate services segment generated $529 million in revenue, up 10% from a year prior. The company as a whole generated $2.28 billion in revenue, a 6% annual increase, and net income of $215 million, up 43% compared to a year prior.

#5462. Los Angeles votes all-in on housing, electing YIMBY-backed Raman

Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles as YIMBY groups framed the race around accelerating housing production. City timelines for statewide SB 79 transit oriented housing rules, currently delayed to 2030, are expected to face pressure under the new administration.  AI Summary

City Councilmember Nithya Raman defeated Mayor Karen Bass to become the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, a win for the “yes in my backyard” groups that backed her challenge to the incumbent.

The Associated Press called the race Thursday. Raman, an urban planner and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, led by 4.2 percentage points, 52.1% to 47.9%, with roughly 76% of the expected vote counted.

She is the second DSA member to lead a major U.S. city. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani won a year ago on an affordability platform that made more housing a focal point. Bass conceded and promised a “smooth and seamless transition.” She is the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a reelection bid.

Raman won despite long odds. Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, retiring former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and nearly every City Council member backed Bass.

YIMBY Action, YIMBY Los Angeles and California YIMBY were among the housing groups behind Raman. Unions, progressive Democratic organizations, environmental groups and County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath also endorsed her.

Housing and homelessness drove the campaign. Raman pitched expanded medical teams for people in encampments and moving residents out of city-rented hotels into permanent housing. She said she could cut encampments by at least half by 2028.

YIMBY groups cast the race as a test of how fast the city builds. The movement pushes to ease zoning limits and speed approvals to expand supply.

“Her win in California’s largest city is a big moment for the pro-housing movement,” California YIMBY posted on social media.

One early test is how Los Angeles complies with Senate Bill 79, the state law that encourages more housing near transit. City ordinances that took effect June 30 hold off full compliance citywide until 2030. YIMBY advocates will likely press the new mayor and council to move that date up. Raman favored a quicker housing timeline.

Mayor-elect Raman could inherit a $20 million-plus liability if the city doesn’t approve Woodland Hills Country Club’s 398-home plan. The club’s attorney, Dave Rand, a Raman supporter, set a 60-day deadline, and the state housing department wants a response by Nov. 25.

Raman will need the council to do that. Most members backed Bass, so Raman must build a majority from a body that largely opposed her.

She will have allies elsewhere at City Hall. Controller Kenneth Mejia and newly elected City Attorney Marissa Roy, a DSA member, join her in what The Hollywood Reporter called a “triumvirate of progressivism” at the top of city government.

#5461. Google Cloud storage moves to the front of the AI stack as enterprises hit the GPU utilization ceiling

ANALYSIS by Paul Nashawaty

For the past two years, enterprise AI investment has been dominated by one conversation: compute. Organizations raced to secure GPU allocations, negotiated infrastructure deals and stood up machine learning platforms at speed. What many discovered only after the fact is that the bottleneck they thought they were solving was not the only one in the room. Storage is now throttling the very accelerators enterprises fought to acquire.

In the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast, I spoke with Ronen Schwartz, vice president of products for Google Cloud Storage at Google LLC, about why storage has quietly become the defining constraint in enterprise AI infrastructure, and what a purpose-built architecture for AI workloads actually looks like. The conversation cuts to a problem that is real, measurable and still largely underacknowledged in most AI strategy discussions.

“Storage just got promoted,” Schwartz said. “Instead of being at the backend as an enabler, it is moving into the front as a critical part of accelerator execution.”

The economics of this problem are direct. Accelerators are, as Schwartz put it, an enterprise’s most expensive line item. Every second they idle waiting for data is money lost — not in some theoretical efficiency calculation, but in immediate, traceable waste. Yet when teams finally get access to their TPUs or GPUs, the data delivery path often hasn’t received the same attention as the compute layer.

“I speak to many customers, and what I’m hearing is the team spent a long time fighting to get their TPUs, their GPUs, to get their hands on accelerators. And once they got them, they’re actually not always able to get the output they needed. Very often it actually goes back to not enough thought put into the data delivery path.”

This is not a fringe scenario. Schwartz described a pattern where organizations identify the storage bottleneck only after it hits them — when GPU utilization metrics fall short of targets and training timelines stretch beyond projections. By then, the cost of underinvesting in storage architecture is already embedded in the project.

One of the clearest insights from the conversation is that AI is not a single workload, and treating it as one creates compounding gaps in storage architecture. Schwartz described training, inference and agentic workloads as having fundamentally different “heartbeats” with distinct data movement patterns that each require targeted design.

Training demands massive sequential reads, but the equally critical pressure point is checkpoint management. Every 15 minutes or so, a training cluster must pause and write a multi-terabyte checkpoint to protect work done against potential failure. “Slow storage in that place freezes the entire GPU cluster,” Schwartz said. Google’s Rapid object storage technology, he noted, can write checkpoints more than three times faster and restore them more than five times faster than standard object storage, and this distinction matters significantly at scale. He pointed to Torin, an autonomous vehicle company, as an example: millions of sensor data points flowing into storage to train vehicle models, where checkpoint performance is not an edge case but a core operational requirement.

Inference introduces a different constraint entirely, that of real-time, latency-sensitive interaction where response time directly affects user experience and token economics. Agentic workloads layer on a third set of demands: shared workspaces, state persistence across agents, low-latency retrieval and the need to support both short-lived and long-running agent processes that may hibernate and reactivate on demand.

“AI is not one workload. Really, the movement of data looks completely different. It’s like different heartbeats depending on where you are in the lifecycle.”

Google’s differentiation argument centers on infrastructure credibility built over years of running hyperscale AI workloads internally before offering the same capabilities externally. Schwartz cited specific performance figures: 15 terabytes per second on Rapid object storage and 10 terabytes per second on Google Cloud managed clusters, which he described as verified industry-leading numbers.

The technical foundation includes zonal colocation, or placing data physically close to GPU and TPU clusters to minimize the time a byte travels to the accelerator. Schwartz described this as a first-to-market capability that required rethinking assumptions baked into traditional storage design, where multi-zone or multi-region distribution was the default goal. For AI workloads, proximity to the accelerator takes priority. Google’s Rapid Bucket technology reduces processing steps in the storage path, enabling a single bucket to deliver more than 15 terabytes per second throughput with support for 20 million queries per second at sub-millisecond latency.

“It is because it is built on the Google infrastructure, which has been used internally longer than anyone else to support accelerators and their performance. But it is also because Google is working with nine out of the ten world-leading AI frontier model companies.” A storage architecture that can demonstrably improve GPU utilization can provide faster iteration through less idle compute and lower effective cost per training run.

The agentic dimension of the conversation revealed an underappreciated wrinkle in enterprise AI readiness. Agents require more than web browsing and database queries; they need access to unstructured data at scale, including images, video, documents and PDFs that represent the bulk of most organizations’ real data assets. Without a way to make that content semantically accessible, agents operate with a restricted and often unrepresentative view of enterprise knowledge.

Google’s response is what Schwartz called a Smart Storage Initiative, anchored by a recently launched Object Enrichment capability. When a file or image lands in a storage bucket, Google AI models automatically extract content and attach structured metadata to the object — in seconds, and at scale. The result is that what was previously unstructured becomes queryable by agents without manual intervention or downstream processing pipelines.

“An agent can now interact with what used to be called unstructured data because there is actually a very good understanding of the content.” The storage layer is also integrated into Google’s broader agentic data cloud and borderless lakehouse architecture, allowing agents to reach data stored outside Google’s environment as well.

For agent infrastructure at scale, Schwartz described dedicated Filestore agent volumes integrated directly into Google Kubernetes Engine and the agent sandbox environment, designed specifically to handle the cost, response speed, and data-sharing requirements of running thousands or millions of agents simultaneously.

The broader market shift here is architectural, not incremental. Enterprise AI infrastructure has been built in layers (compute first, then frameworks, then data) and storage was often treated as a procurement checkbox rather than a performance variable. That sequencing is proving costly. As GPU utilization targets become measurable KPIs and AI operations budgets face tighter scrutiny, the storage layer is being reassessed in a way it hasn’t been in years.

What Google’s position illustrates is that hyperscale operational experience at the storage layer translates directly into enterprise advantage — not as a marketing claim, but as a measurable difference in checkpoint speed, throughput, latency and agent responsiveness. The companies that have been running frontier model training and inference at scale have been forced to solve these problems; enterprise teams are now encountering them for the first time.

For platform engineers, ML infrastructure teams and enterprise architects, the implication is specific: Storage architecture decisions made during initial AI platform buildout will constrain or enable performance for every workload that follows. Revisiting those decisions after the bottleneck appears is significantly more expensive than addressing them in the design phase.

The market is heading toward a point where AI infrastructure conversations routinely include storage as a primary tier, not an afterthought. Organizations that recognize that shift early will extract measurably more value from the accelerator investments they have already made.

To hear the full conversation with Ronen Schwartz, check out the latest episode of the AppDevANGLE podcast. To learn more about how Google Cloud Storage can support the evolving demands of enterprise AI, explore Google’s storage solutions or connect with the Google Cloud team to discuss the right approach for your organization’s workloads.

#5459. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5458. Tucows Reports Third Quarter Results In Line with Expectations with Progress on Balance Sheet Obligations

TORONTO, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tucows Inc. (NASDAQ: TCX) (TSX: TC), a global internet services leader, today reported its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026. All figures are in U.S. dollars.

"Adjusted EBITDA and gross profit grew year over year, and we remain on track for our 2026 guidance," said David Woroch, President and Chief Executive Officer of Tucows. "We also retired the Ting preferred units valued at $149.3 million, and repaid $6 million on our syndicated loan facility. After quarter end, we agreed to assign Ting's Colorado Springs lease, which is expected to release Tucows' parent guaranty in the spring. Each of these steps makes the business simpler and more flexible than it was a quarter ago."

Gross profit for the third quarter of 2026 increased 20.5% to $29.1 million from the third quarter of 2025, and improved 13% sequentially. Both the year-over-year and sequential expansion was driven primarily by a large, non-recurring re-rate from the renegotiation of our mobile contract within the Corporate segment, as well as year-over-year growth from Ting.

We ended the third quarter of 2026 with cash and cash equivalents, and restricted cash and restricted cash equivalents of $41.0 million. This compares with $60.2 million at the end of the second quarter of 2026 and $70.8 million at the end of the third quarter of 2025.

#5456. NEAR Protocol Tokenomics Overhaul Catapults The Crypto Coin 10% Higher

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

NEAR Protocol is climbing as the market weighs a major tokenomics overhaul designed to reduce token inflation and ease long-term selling pressure. The NEAR rally follows crypto governance approval of a proposal to lower the network’s annual issuance ceiling from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years.

The proposal, known as HSP-029, passed with overwhelming support from NEAR’s House of Stake. It would gradually reduce the number of new tokens entering circulation, potentially strengthening the supply outlook as the network expands.

NEAR Plans to Take Millions of Tokens Out of Future IssuanceNEAR Protocol's (@NEARProtocol) $NEAR House of Stake has approved a proposal to reduce maximum annual token issuance from 2.5% to 1.6%.The change will roll out gradually over 24 months, reducing the issuance ceiling… pic.twitter.com/pmPOUrWhoI

The move comes as NEAR Protocol seeks to turn its growing ecosystem activity into stronger value for token holders. With issuance cuts, cross-chain infrastructure, and renewed trading interest converging, we are watching if NEAR can sustain its latest breakout.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The approved proposal would reduce NEAR’s maximum annual issuance rate from 2.5% to 1.6%, with the change phased in over 24 months. According to the proposal, the reduction could prevent 11.8 million NEAR from entering circulation during the first two years. Over six years, the avoided issuance could reach 66.1 million tokens.

At full implementation, daily issuance would fall from roughly 89,500 NEAR to 57,300 NEAR. The network would retain its existing distribution of newly issued tokens, with 90% going to staking participants and 10% allocated to the protocol treasury.

The overhaul also introduces a trade-off for stakers. Gross staking yields could decline from approximately 5.27% to 3.37%, assuming staking participation remains unchanged.

However, the proposal still requires Security Council review, a 90-day grace period, and validator adoption before the changes become binding.

Beyond tokenomics, NEAR Protocol continues developing its chain-signature technology, which allows accounts to interact with external blockchains. NEAR Intents also supports cross-chain swaps, giving the ecosystem another potential source of activity and fee revenue.

The combination of lower issuance and expanding utility is giving NEAR crypto bulls a fresh narrative. However, the market will need to see sustained demand before the supply reduction translates into a lasting price trend.

NEAR Protocol’s cross-chain ambitions arrive as Bitcoin infrastructure projects compete to bring more functionality to the world’s largest cryptocurrency.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning itself as a Bitcoin Layer-2 network designed to support faster transactions, lower fees, and smart-contract functionality. Its architecture aims to connect Bitcoin’s security and liquidity with applications typically associated with more flexible blockchain ecosystems.

Bitcoin Hyper has begun rolling out testnet infrastructure, including a wallet and explorer, as it prepares for broader network testing.

Did somebody order a little extra Bitcoin utility? 👀⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4FWNQ pic.twitter.com/bQAMiOcdUD

While NEAR Protocol is building cross-chain functionality across multiple networks, Bitcoin Hyper is focusing directly on expanding Bitcoin’s role in decentralized finance. This could become important if Bitcoin holders increasingly seek access to applications, trading, and other on-chain opportunities without moving away from BTC-focused infrastructure.

The project is approaching its planned November 26, 2026, launch, with its presale entering the final stretch. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.2 million, while HYPER is priced at just $0.0136.

The project also offers staking rewards of 35% APY, adding another incentive for early participants ahead of its anticipated token launch.

With the presale scheduled to end on November 26, the approaching launch is becoming a key milestone for HYPER holders watching for exchange listings and ecosystem growth.

NEAR crypto is trading around the $3.80 area, leaving the $4 level as an important near-term hurdle. A sustained move above $4 could strengthen the recovery narrative and open the door toward the $4.30 region. A stronger breakout could bring the $4.50 area into focus, particularly if broader altcoin sentiment improves.

The tokenomics overhaul gives bulls a fundamental catalyst, but traders will also need to see stronger spot demand and improving market momentum.

On the downside, a failure to hold the $3.70–$3.80 area could expose NEAR to another test of support near $3.50. Continued weakness across the broader crypto market would make a sustained recovery more difficult.

For now, NEAR Protocol has a clear catalyst in its issuance reduction proposal, alongside continued development of its cross-chain ecosystem. The next stage of the crypto rally depends on whether buyers can turn the tokenomics story into sustained demand and push NEAR beyond its immediate resistance levels.

#5455. webAI Launches webAI App for On-Device AI With No Per-Token Charges

The webAI app lets anyone build teams of AI experts that work across Slack, DocuSign, Hugging Face, Apple apps and more, while their files stay on their Mac.

AUSTIN, Texas, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- webAI today released the webAI app for Mac to the public for the first time. The app runs webAI's new small reasoning models on the user's own computer, so people can use AI on private work without sending files to the cloud or paying per token.

Most AI runs in the cloud, where usage is metered by tokens or capped by plan, and every document goes to someone else's servers. webAI runs the model on the Mac itself. A user can work through a sensitive client proposal or an unfinished business plan, revise it as many times as they want, and never hit a token limit.

"With the webAI app, we're making cloud AI optional," said David Stout, CEO and co-founder of webAI. "Why should you have to send a private document to an online service just to get help with it? Your Mac can do the work. You keep control of what you share, and you can ask as many follow-up questions as you need without watching a token meter."

In the app, users create Personas: AI experts with a role, knowledge and tools the user chooses. Several Personas can work together on the same task. A consultant could have one pull client requirements from project notes, a second draft the proposal and a third check the draft for anything missed.

Connectors work with the apps you already use, including Slack, DocuSign, Hugging Face and Apple apps. You control what each Persona can access and what actions it can take. A Persona can pull a client's latest decisions from Slack, see which contracts are still unsigned in DocuSign, and draft follow-ups for your approval. You spend less time hunting for context and copying details between apps.

Watch the demo: https://www.webai.com/blog/webai-launches-webai-app-for-on-device-ai-with-no-per-token-charges

Availability: The webAI app is available now for Mac at webAI.com.
