#5434. 10 world leaders ranked by salary, from Australia's PM to Spain's head of government

Free daily briefing on global business news.

See how 10 world leaders' salaries compare in U.S. dollars and against the minimum wage paid to workers in their own countries.

Every national leader cashes a paycheck that the public funds, and the sum draws scrutiny from the people footing the bill. Citizens who argue about wages, taxes, and the cost of living want to know whether the person in charge shares their economic reality or occupies a different one. The question carries weight beyond curiosity. A leader's compensation can signal how a country values public office. It also offers a rough gauge of the distance between those who govern and those who earn the legal wage floor. Lining up those paychecks across borders creates a puzzle of its own. Each country sets the amount in a separate currency and under separate laws.

Converting every salary into U.S. dollars yields a neat table, yet the result says more about exchange rates and the size of each economy than about the job itself. A different yardstick cuts closer to the issue readers raise. Dividing a leader's annual salary by the local full-time minimum wage shows how many of the country's lowest-paid workers it would take to match the person at the top. The measure keeps every comparison inside a single economy, with one currency and one set of prices. It can reshuffle the order a dollar ranking produces, lifting some countries and pulling others down. Salary and wealth differ, too. A generous salary does not equal a large net worth. The numbers that follow track what each office pays. They say nothing about what any officeholder owns.

Neto gathered pay figures for 10 leaders, limiting the list to those whose 2026 earnings it could confirm through an official source. Germany's chancellor fell outside the list for lack of such a confirmed amount. The publication orders the 10 by approximate U.S. dollar value and expresses each total as a multiple of the local full-time minimum wage. Several entries depart from the 2026 baseline. France's total comes from a presidential payslip dated January 2024, which the publication expects has not changed. Spain's reflects the sum disbursed in 2025. Mexico's total folds in the year-end bonus and benefits. The bundled total and the base salaries elsewhere measure different things. Italy's entry rests on parliamentary pay.

Australia's prime minister commands A$622,102 a year, about US$433,900 and the largest dollar sum of any leader on this list. The figure begins with the A$239,270 salary every federal parliamentarian receives. The office layers on another 160%, or A$382,832, which turns a lawmaker's standard pay into the richest package in the group.

The premium by itself outstrips the parliamentary salary by A$143,562, a margin equal to 60% of that salary. Holding the office supplies 61.5% of the total, and the seat in parliament provides the other 38.5%. Put another way, the top job pays 2.6 times what an ordinary member earns. The loading alone comes to roughly US$267,000, more than the entire annual pay of Britain's prime minister or any leader below that entry. The standard parliamentary salary, valued near US$166,900, would by itself exceed the full packages of the leaders of Mexico, Italy, Brazil, and Spain.

Australia's Remuneration Tribunal, an independent body, sets the base salary on which the prime minister's pay rests. The tribunal said that federal politicians' pay had to be fair and comparable with other earnings. It added that the level had to draw in and retain capable people. Any shift in the base passes through the 160% loading. Each extra dollar there adds A$2.60 to the prime minister's pay.

The prime minister's pay equals 12 times what a full-time worker on Australia's minimum wage earns, a smaller multiple than the presidents of the U.S., Mexico, and Brazil post despite their lower dollar totals. Working back from the multiple puts the full-time wage floor near A$51,800 a year. The parliamentary salary on its own runs to about 4.6 times that floor. A wage floor of that size keeps the gap between Australia's top office and its lowest-paid full-time workers near the middle of the group, even as the dollar figure exceeds every other leader's.

The U.S. president receives $400,000 a year, 27 times the pay of a full-time worker on the federal minimum wage. The salary appears in federal statute as a fixed dollar amount. Raising it would mean rewriting the law itself.

A $50,000 expense allowance arrives on top of the base pay, lifting the full package to $450,000. Counting the allowance, the total reaches about 30 times a full-time federal minimum-wage income. The salary alone falls about $33,900 short of the Australian prime minister's converted pay, the single entry on the list worth more in dollars. The gap between the two top earners amounts to less than a tenth of the U.S. figure.

Former presidents keep collecting public money after they leave office. Their pension matches a Cabinet secretary's pay, which stands at $253,100 in 2026. Departing the job trims the yearly payment by $146,900 from the presidential salary. The benefit equals about 63% of a sitting president's pay and about 17 times what a full-time federal minimum-wage worker takes in over a year. Even in retirement, a former president outpaces the lowest-paid full-time worker by a wide margin.

The federal minimum wage accounts for much of the 27-times gap. It has stayed at $7.25 an hour since 2009, which works out to about $15,080 a year for full-time work. The floor has gone 17 years without an increase as of 2026. A wage stuck that long will inflate any ratio that uses it as the divisor.

Most states set a higher minimum of their own. A full-time worker in one of those states makes more than $15,080 a year, which pulls that worker's multiple below 27. Neto attributes the extreme U.S. showing on this measure to the federal rate. The 27-times multiple tracks a stalled federal wage floor as much as it tracks the size of the presidential paycheck.

Canada's prime minister earns C$435,400 a year, about US$305,300, under pay rates that took effect April 1, 2026. The sum splits into two equal halves. A seat in the House of Commons brings C$217,700, and leading the government adds an identical C$217,700. In euros, the package is worth about €273,000. Canada prices the premiership at one more legislator's paycheck, no more and no less.

Britain's and Ireland's leaders pair a legislative salary with pay for the top office, though the two pieces differ in size in each country. Canada's matching halves leave no ambiguity about the premium. Taking charge of the government doubles what a member of Parliament earns.

Canada's federal minimum wage climbed to C$18.15 an hour in April 2026, the same month the new parliamentary pay began. A worker earning that wage across a full-time year collects about C$37,750. The prime minister's total equals 11.5 times that income. Measured by the hour over the same full-time year, the leader's pay works out to about C$209, set against the C$18.15 floor.

Each half of the package would amount to nearly six times a full-time minimum wage income on its own. The parliamentary salary by itself clears the floor by a wide margin. The supplement for running the government repeats that distance a second time.

Canada's total sits third among the 10 leaders in dollar terms, behind Australia and the U.S. Canada's leader trails the U.S. president by about US$94,700, yet Canada's multiple comes to less than half the American one. The two leaders stand closer together in currency than in their separation from the lowest-paid worker at home.

Australia's prime minister collects about US$128,600 more than Canada's, but the minimum wage multiples of the two countries differ by half a point. A full-time Canadian minimum wage income equals about 8.7% of the prime minister's annual pay.

Ireland's Taoiseach earns €256,311 a year, about US$286,600, and the total stacks two separate lines of pay. A TD salary of €119,467 forms the base. The office of Taoiseach adds €136,844 on top of the seat in parliament. Both rates took effect June 1, 2026.

The leadership portion outstrips the parliamentary share by €17,377. Running the government accounts for about 53.4% of the package. Canada divides its prime minister's earnings into two identical halves. Ireland tilts the balance toward the office, attaching a sum worth about 115% of the TD rate. The design attaches more money to leading the country than to holding a seat.

The Taoiseach's income equals nine times what a full-time minimum-wage worker in Ireland makes in a year. Five of the nine leaders whose countries set a statutory minimum wage show a wider gap: Australia, Canada, the U.S., Mexico, and Brazil. Ireland's drop from fourth on dollar value to sixth on this yardstick suggests its lowest-paid full-time workers stand closer to their leader than counterparts in those five countries stand to theirs. Canada offers the sharpest contrast. The Canadian prime minister outearns the Taoiseach in dollars and also sits farther from the country's wage floor.

Ireland's leader also outpaces every other European entry on the list in dollar terms. France, the U.K., and Spain each post a smaller multiple of the minimum wage, and Italy sets no statutory floor at all. Among the European entries, Ireland pairs the biggest dollar paycheck with the widest gap between the head of government and the lowest-paid worker.

A few Irish office holders hand back part of their pay. As a result, the €256,311 figure reflects an entitlement, and the sum reaching any given holder may come in lower.

The Taoiseach supplement by itself exceeds the entire sum Spain paid its head of government in 2025.

Britain's prime minister earns £174,039 for 2026-27, about US$230,300, even after turning down part of the pay attached to the top job. The ministerial entitlement stands at £83,837 a year. The prime minister claims £75,440 of it and leaves £8,397 unclaimed. As a result, the office holder accepts about 90% of the available sum.

Claiming the full amount would lift the annual package to £182,436. The unclaimed portion looks small against a six-figure income. Even so, the figures list the entitlement and the claim as two separate numbers, which marks the lower amount as a choice the office holder makes.

A seat in Parliament supplies the larger slice of the money. The £98,599 MP salary accounts for about 57% of the package. In practice, the parliamentary role pays more than the prime ministerial one. The imbalance would persist even with the full entitlement in hand, because £98,599 still exceeds £83,837 by £14,762.

Britain splits the money in the opposite direction from Canada and Australia. Canada pays its prime minister the same amount for leading the government as for serving as an MP. Australia's top-up exceeds the base parliamentary salary. Britain's claimed ministerial pay equals about 77% of the MP salary, and even the full entitlement reaches only about 85%.

The British premier's pay equals about seven times the local full-time minimum wage, a narrow spread by the standards of this list. Neto pairs the U.K. with Spain as the two countries with the smallest gaps, both sitting around six to seven times. France's president, one spot lower in dollar terms, shows a wider multiple than Britain.

The decision to claim less feeds into the narrow spread. A smaller claim shrinks the package, and a smaller package pulls the multiple down. The distance between the office and the lowest-paid full-time worker owes part of its modesty to the prime minister's restraint.

France's president grossed €16,039.71 a month in January 2024, and 12 such payments add up to €192,477 a year. The salary equals about US$215,200, which slots France below Britain and above Mexico among the 10 leaders. The annual total matches 12 identical monthly installments, with none of the extra 13th payment Brazil's president receives.

The president collects 8.6 times the annual earnings of a full-time worker on France's minimum wage. Working backward from that ratio puts the French wage floor near €22,400 a year. Ireland's Taoiseach stands at nine times while drawing about US$71,400 more in dollars. Dividing the Irish total by nine yields a floor close to €28,500. The eurozone neighbor guarantees its lowest earners about €6,100 more each year than France does.

Britain's prime minister earns about US$15,100 more than the French president yet sits at seven times the local minimum wage, a tighter distance from the bottom of the scale. France's smaller salary and wider multiple mean Britain's floor runs higher in dollar terms. The same arithmetic puts the British minimum near US$32,900 a year, against some US$25,000 for France.

France, Ireland, and Britain form a European cluster of single-digit multiples, far from the U.S. at 27 and Brazil at 29. The French gap amounts to less than a third of the American one. France's salary also exceeds Mexico's full presidential package, bonus and benefits included, by about US$58,100. Yet Mexico's president sits at 25 times the local minimum wage, close to triple the French ratio. France pays its president more in dollars than Mexico does, yet the French salary stays far closer to its country's lowest legal wage.

France's civil service pay scales have stayed frozen since July 2023. Any increase in the French minimum wage would pull the 8.6 multiple down as long as the president's monthly gross holds at €16,039.71.

Mexico's president takes home MX$134,290 a month after deductions, and the full yearly package reaches MX$2,882,131, equal to some US$157,100 or €140,500, once the year-end bonus and benefits join base pay. The monthly net figure has held at that level since 2025.

Twelve months of net pay add up to MX$1,611,480, or 56% of the annual total. The remaining 44% stays outside the monthly deposit. A president reading a pay stub sees a little more than half of what the office delivers over a year.

Mexico's total pay equals 25 times the local full-time minimum wage, which puts a full year at that wage near MX$115,000. A single month of the president's net pay outstrips what a minimum-wage worker earns across 12 months.

The Mexican gap comes close to the American one on a dollar amount less than half the size. The U.S. president's US$400,000 salary is more than 2.5 times Mexico's compensation, yet the American multiple of 27 sits two above Mexico's. Canada offers a sharper contrast. Its prime minister earns 1.9 times as much as Mexico's president in dollar terms, while the Canadian multiple of 11.5 comes to less than half of Mexico's.

Mexico's earnings come in below the dollar pay of six other leaders on the list, yet the president's distance from the lowest-paid full-time worker trails only Brazil and the U.S. The total edges past Italy's US$140,000, the next figure down, by US$17,100. Dollar totals, in Mexico's case, understate how far the president stands from the country's minimum-wage earners.

A federal law governing public servants' pay in Mexico bars anyone in public service from earning more than the president. As a result, the president's salary sets a legal ceiling for the whole state payroll. A freeze at the top holds that ceiling in place for every other official on the government payroll.

Giorgia Meloni draws €0 as Italy's prime minister, and all €125,220 of her official annual pay, worth about US$140,000, flows from her seat in parliament. She stands alone among the 10 leaders as the one whose head-of-government post pays nothing.

Meloni has declared that she accepts no salary for running the government. Italian law bars a prime minister from adding the government salary to an MP's wage. The rule keeps the two incomes from merging into one larger package, and she retains only her parliamentary earnings.

Canada's prime minister, Ireland's Taoiseach, and Britain's prime minister each collect a government salary on top of parliamentary pay, the doubling Italian law rules out. Each of them brings home two paychecks for the same dual role Meloni holds. Italy's arrangement leaves her with one.

Her parliamentary salary amounts to €10,435 gross each month, plus allowances. Twelve months at that rate produce €125,220, which shows the annual figure counts base salary alone. The allowances lift her income from public office above that total, by an amount the list leaves undisclosed.

Meloni's legislative wage by itself outstrips the full packages of two other leaders on the list, Brazil's president and Spain's head of government. Italy and Spain both pay in euros, which strips exchange rates out of the second comparison. Her MP salary runs €29,276 above what the Spanish leader received in 2025.

Italy has no statutory minimum wage, which leaves Meloni as the only leader on the list without a pay multiple. The other nine entries each show how many times their leader out-earns a full-time worker on the legal floor. Italy supplies no such benchmark, and the distance between her pay and the bottom of its labor market goes unmeasured.

Italian taxpayers fund Meloni at a lawmaker's rate, and the premiership adds nothing to the bill. Her eighth-place spot in the dollar ordering reflects a legislative wage.

Brazil's president takes in R$602,760 a year, about US$120,700, a sum 29 times the country's minimum wage and the widest gap among the 10 leaders. A worker on that minimum would need about 29 years of full-time labor to earn what the president collects in one.

The money arrives in 13 installments of R$46,366.19, one more payment than the calendar has months. A single installment equals about 28.6 times the R$1,621 minimum wage set for 2026. The gap stays about as wide paycheck by paycheck as it does across the full year.

Brazil's dollar total sits ninth of 10, ahead of only Spain's head of government at US$107,300. A margin of US$13,400 separates the two sums, yet Spain's leader receives 5.6 times the local minimum wage, a ratio less than one-fifth the size of Brazil's. Two salaries close in dollars can rest on wage floors far apart.

Australia's prime minister and the U.S. president each collect more than three times Brazil's dollar sum, at US$433,900 and US$400,000. Canada's prime minister brings in about US$305,300, some two and a half times the Brazilian amount. All three trail Brazil on the ratio, with multiples of 12, 27, and 11.5. Europe sharpens the contrast. Ireland's Taoiseach posts the highest European multiple at nine, and Brazil's figure exceeds triple that level.

The Americas hold the widest gaps. Brazil, the U.S., and Mexico account for the three largest multiples, at 29, 27, and 25. Mexico's president outearns Brazil's in dollars, at about US$157,100 with benefits included, yet falls behind on the ratio. Mexico's figure also counts benefits, so Brazil's edge on the ratio survives against a broader measure of pay. Neto notes that some Latin American countries beyond these 10 show a wider gap. Brazil's top office looks modest to anyone tallying dollars and lavish to anyone earning the legal minimum, a split wider than any other leader's on the list.

Spain's president of the government received €95,944 in 2025, about US$107,300, the smallest dollar sum attached to any of the 10 leaders on the list.

Spain's salary trails the leaders above it by a wide margin. In dollars, it comes to about one-quarter of the Australian prime minister's pay and less than one-third of the U.S. president's federal salary. Brazil's president, the nearest leader in dollar terms, collects about US$13,400 more.

Four leaders on the list draw pay in euros, which strips exchange rates out of the comparison. Spain's €95,944 sits about €29,300 below the €125,220 Italy's prime minister receives from her parliamentary seat. France's president grosses €192,477 a year, about double the Spanish figure. Ireland's Taoiseach collects €256,311, more than two and a half times as much. Spain's leader is the only one of the four paid less than €100,000.

Spain's leader also sits closer to the country's lowest-paid full-time workers than any other leader with a minimum wage comparison, at 5.6 times the local minimum wage. Neto pairs Spain with the U.K. as the two countries showing the narrowest gaps, putting both at around 6 to 7 times. Britain's prime minister lands at 7 times, France's president at 8.6, and Ireland's Taoiseach at 9.

Brazil's president stands more than five times as far from that country's wage floor as Spain's leader does. Mexico's president sits nearly four and a half times as far. The U.S. president, at 27 times, stands nearly five times as far.

No other leader lands at the same end of both scales. Australia's prime minister collects the most in dollars, yet three other leaders show a wider gap to their own minimum wage. Brazil's president sits ninth in dollar terms despite the widest gap. Spain's head of government stays at the bottom on either yardstick, which makes the post the most modest on the list measured against foreign peers and against Spanish workers alike.

#5433. Block DOJ Settlement: Jack Dorsey’s Company Faces $764M Deal as Bitcoin Profit Plunges 50%

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Block DOJ settlement talks have reached a major turning point, with Jack Dorsey-owned payments company agreeing in principle to pay $764 million. The proposed deal would resolve a federal investigation into alleged failures in its anti-money laundering controls.

The agreement follows years of scrutiny over Block’s Cash App compliance practices. The company disclosed the development in its quarterly filing yesterday, outlining a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice.

Jack Dorsey’s Block has beaten Q3 earnings estimates, posting $3.2B in gross profit.The company has also raised its 2026 outlook, while warning that a potential DOJ settlement could be larger than expected.Strong results and a higher forecast from one of the biggest names in… pic.twitter.com/Bk0KByUDPV

The announcement arrives alongside a sharp decline in Block’s Bitcoin business. Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit plunged 50% year-over-year to $52 million during the third quarter, despite stronger overall company earnings.

The proposed Block DOJ agreement would defer prosecution for three years over allegations that the company failed to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. The DOJ’s investigation centers on compliance requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act. Block would need to meet obligations outlined in the agreement throughout its term.

If the company fully complies, prosecutors would move to dismiss the deferred charges. However, the resolution remains subject to final agreement terms and court approval.

The proposed settlement carries a gross monetary component of approximately $964 million. Credits for previous regulatory resolutions would reduce the expected net payment to roughly $764 million. Block has already accrued $764 million for the matter as of September 30. The company warned that the final cost could exceed that amount.

The investigation dates back to 2023, when federal authorities began examining Block’s compliance practices and related disclosures. The scrutiny followed allegations raised by short seller Hindenburg Research.

Block rejected those allegations as inaccurate and misleading. Separately, New York’s financial regulator fined the company $40 million in 2025 over compliance failures.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The Block DOJ development comes as the company’s Bitcoin business faces a sharp profitability decline. Block reported Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit of $52 million in Q3, down from $104 million a year earlier. The company attributed the decline primarily to lower fees on certain Bitcoin transactions through Cash App.

Bitcoin-related revenue reached approximately $1.8 billion during the quarter. However, the lower fees significantly reduced the amount Block retained from its Bitcoin operations.

The weakness contrasts with stronger performance across the broader business. Block reported $3.24 billion in total gross profit, up 22% year-over-year. Cash App gross profit climbed 27% to $2.07 billion. Square gross profit increased 14%, while quarterly net income rose to approximately $566 million.

Block also raised its full-year 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, representing expected growth of roughly 22%.

Now, proposed Block DOJ settlement creates a major legal expense alongside a mixed earnings picture. Its Bitcoin business is generating less profit, even as Cash App and Square support stronger company-wide growth.

#5432. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5431. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

#5430. Google is building its first Wyoming data center in a $17 billion deal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Laramie County project will draw power from a 702-megawatt natural gas fuel cell plant with carbon capture

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Alphabet $GOOGL's Google announced plans for its first data center in Wyoming on Thursday, a $17 billion investment in Laramie County. The company is working on the project with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power $AEP (AEP) and Related Digital.

Google said it will cover the full cost of the electricity consumed at the facility, along with any infrastructure demands that its expansion generates. The data center will rely on air cooling rather than water, easing pressure on local supplies.

The project is contracted with AEP for a 702-megawatt fuel cell development that runs on natural gas, with fuel cells made by Bloom Energy. Google said carbon capture and storage will trap a large majority of the plant's emissions at Tallgrass's Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub. Google has not disclosed what percentage that represents, according to The Next Web.

Google is also drawing electricity from natural gas facilities that Tallgrass and Black Hills Energy operate. It is conducting an engineering and design study on fitting Tallgrass's combined cycle turbines with carbon capture technology.

Black Hills said in an Oct. 6 release that it had signed definitive agreements, effective Sept. 30, to serve the planned data center. The company plans to invest $1.8 billion between 2027 and 2029 to build 564 MW of natural gas generation. It will provide up to 590 MW of grid-connected service and manage 2.1 GW of third-party contracted resources through a private microgrid.

Black Hills said energy service is planned to begin in late 2027 and ramp to peak load in 2030. The company expects the project to provide an estimated $150 million of net income in 2030.

Google anticipates that the project will deliver local property tax revenue worth several hundred million dollars to Laramie County and School District 1. It met with more than 200 county residents at a community meeting in downtown Cheyenne, where attendees voiced unease over the effect of data center expansion on the city. Google, its partners and Bloom Energy are forming a Community Council to develop solutions for Cheyenne.

AEP said in October it plans to invest approximately $4 billion in the fuel cell plant under a 20-year power purchase agreement with Google. Full operations are expected by the end of 2028.

Crusoe announced the Wyoming project with Tallgrass in July 2025, according to Bloomberg. Crusoe was sidelined from the project in June when Google voiced worries over expenses and scheduling, according to Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources. Black Hills said it was pressing ahead without Crusoe.

The announcement came two days after voters across the U.S. approved restrictions on data centers in 40 of the 41 local ballot measures put to them, according to The Next Web.

#5429. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5426. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5424. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5422. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?
